#4874. Fall Weddings Are More Popular Than Ever. Here's How to Dress for One (The Right Way)

Autumn is now the most popular season to tie the knot.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WEDDINGS CAN be hard to dress for, and this isn’t limited to those directly involved; being a mere attendant requires some degree of planning. I’ve attended quite a few weddings over the last year, both as a groomsman and as a regular guest, both with their own sartorial challenges. (I actually found it more stressful not being in the wedding party, at least in one aspect: I had to pick out my own outfit. This also allowed for a little creativity.)

I covered some options for summer weddings a few months back, and just like that, we’re on to the next season. Fall has arguably become the season for weddings; in fact, October recently overtook June as the most popular month for weddings in the U.S. I can attest to this; I was in two separate ones last October.

Summer and fall weddings have quite a few differences. You can get away with some more “fun” looks in the summer, and you can get a little more creative with the materials (linen, seersucker, etc.). Fall weddings are typically a little more buttoned-up, but there’s a little wiggle room there, too.

I’ll go through some of the easiest ways for guys to dress for an autumn affair—with different wedding types in mind—to get you off the ground. We also included plenty of price points because, as everyone knows, weddings can get expensive fast.

Brooks Brothers Explorer Collection Non-Iron Twill Button Down Collar

Cole Haan Men's Grand Neoclassic Plain Toe Oxfords

We’ll start with what we consider a traditional wedding: a separate ceremony at a church, chapel, or the wedding venue without a black-tie dress code. This is about as classic as it gets, so you don’t have to go overboard—but we do recommend wearing a timeless suit. Our style team has tested plenty of affordable menswear brands offering solid options that approximate the look and fit of made-to-measure tailoring. One of them is the Black Tux, an upstart that offers suits for both rental and purchase, with virtual and in-person fittings to match you with the closest standard size. The prices are great, too: the Essential Suit is just under $300 all in. We also happened to score a 20 percent off code for the Black Tux, made exclusively for Men’s Health readers. Just use code MH20 at checkout (minimum of $295). The code’s good until October 31. Most of its higher-priced suits also include a rental option, but for the extra $100 or so, we’d recommend just buying one. The True Navy is a safe color you can wear year-round. The Grey Suit is a step up and is made from a heavier—but still breathable—merino wool. Perfect for the autumn temperatures.

A classic dress shirt is more than okay, but if you want to stand out in an otherwise pretty basic look, you can go with a classic twill dress shirt like this one from Brooks Brothers. You can get a little bit more creative with the tie, but nothing too crazy; the left-to-right diagonal stripes of a classic rep tie keep it distinguished. A Classic Textured Solid Tie is always a safe bet, too. Baby blue and pink go well with a gray suit, and navy, black, and red look better with gray. The shoes are easy, too: black plain-toe oxfords for grays, and these simple brown Astorflex Loafers with a crisp navy blue.

Brooks Brothers Classic Fit Double-Breasted Wool Pinstripe 1818 Suit

Charles Tyrwhitt Cotton Pocket Square - White

Mack Weldon Silver Extended Crew Dress Sock

The Black Tux Picture Frame Brushed Gold Tie Bar

Black-tie affairs probably require even less creativity, but there are definitely ways to push the envelope to stand out. The safe choice, of course, is the classic tux. If you plan to need one on multiple occasions, we also love that the Black Tux once again gets top marks; its Essential option is also under $300. There are some pricier options you can also rent, but the Essential Tux is low-key enough to rock at any formal occasion. SuitShop is another upstart offering ready-to-wear tuxedos at accessible prices, including several options under $300. Accessories-wise, you can opt for a super fancy pair of onyx cufflinks from one of our favorite watch brands, Shinola, but something a little more budget-friendly is more than okay.

Nowadays, you don’t have to go all-black, at least depending on the event. But if you do deviate, you'd better make it count. Like upgrading to a double-breasted suit, for example. The Classic Fit Double-Breasted Wool Pinstripe 1818 Suit elevates your look without making you look like a Prohibition-era mobster (surprisingly, a very fine line).

The other big component of all of this: your shoes. You probably don’t want to go with a loafer; an oxford or derby shoe is the better option. Our favorite: Cole Haan’s Hawthorne Oxfords, a classic dress shoe that’s made with the brand’s famously comfortable insoles so your dogs will stay happy for hours. It’s also versatile enough to wear at dressy events or in a more casual office vibe. In other words, you’ll be getting a lot of use out of it.

If you want to go all out, you can go full custom. Go big or go home, as they say. If you’re in the NYC area, Alan David Custom is a great choice. The bespoke tailor will give you a sample suit to try on before making final decisions, and the experience is a throwback to classier times. They’ll even ship it to you when it’s all said and done. If you want to go fully custom, you’ll also need the shoes to match.

Bonobos Empire Stretch Italian Wool Tuxedo

Todd Snyder Italian Lightweight Sutton Jacket

Quince Supima Cotton Herringbone Dress Shirt

Todd Snyder Relaxed Fit Japanese Selvedge Chino

Reigning Champ Stretch Chino Marina Standard Pant

Allen Edmonds Rhett Cap-toe Oxford Dress Shoe

Cocktail weddings give you a little more freedom than a traditional one. Here, you can rock a classic suit or a nice blazer and slacks, and you wouldn’t be wrong either way. The classic Ludlow tux from J.Crew gives off serious old-school cocktail jacket vibes, and it’s reserved for swankier occasions. Todd Snyder’s Italian Lightweight Sutton Jacket is another high-end option that’s both breathable and easy to wear throughout the night. If you wear blazers regularly, you’ll also get plenty of use out of this, even into the hotter months. Todd Snyder also makes our favorite pair of relaxed-fit chinos that check a lot of boxes for us. The Relaxed Fit Japanese Selvedge Chino is a steep departure from the ones we wear to the office, which is why it’s such a legit option for dressier occasions.

If the baggier fit (and higher price tag) is scaring you off a bit, Reigning Champ makes an ultra-breathable cotton-twill chino that wears more like a standard dress pant. They’re comfortable, breathable, and have a little added stretch; you’ll get a lot of use out of them outside the wedding. The other big component of all of this: your shoes. You probably don’t want to go with a loafer; an Oxford or derby shoe is the better option. Our style team loves Allen Edmonds’. It’s made with calfskin leather, with a surprisingly light-yet-cushioned outsole that’s comfortable enough to use all night.

Billy Reid Exploded Glen Plaid Archie Jacket

Brooks Brothers Straight-Fit Cotton Advantage Chino Pants

Brooks Brothers Friday Shirt, Oxford Patterns

Madewell Johnny-Collar Sweater Polo in Slub Knit Cotton

Cole Haan Zerogrand Remastered Wing Tip Oxford

Barns have since had a huge come-up and are now a hugely popular wedding venue. Regardless of your stance on barn weddings, you have to dress a little differently. Vineyard weddings (and really any outdoor event) live in that same category. If you’re looking at a late-fall event, you’ll want something a little warmer. The Grey Plaid Wool Suit is a step up in that department without being too overbearing; the subtle designs also scream fall. You can also go with the blazer-and-dress-pants route. Abercrombie’s A&F Collins Blazer is a fantastic budget option, and the Olive Stripe colorway similarly gives off fall vibes. It’s easy to pair with dressier chinos, like the Straight-Fit Cotton Advantage Chino Pants from Brooks Brothers. They’re essentially dress pants with a certain chinoesque comfort.

If you do go this route, you can have a little fun with the undershirt; Brooks Brothers’ Friday Shirt can add some flair to your getup. Madewell’s Johnny-Collar Sweater Polo is also a nice departure from your traditional button-down (and a lot more comfortable, too). If the wedding isn’t all that fancy, you can get away with rocking some of the most comfortable dress shoes/sneakers out there: Cole Haan’s Zerogrand Remastered Wing Tip Oxfords.

Buck Mason Capitola Linen Carry-On Jacket

Bonobos Stretch Weekday Warrior Dress Pants

Reigning Champ Heavyweight Jersey OG T-Shirt

The destination wedding can definitely be a challenge, depending on how close you are to the person (or people) getting married. They’re always a great time, though, and you can get similarly creative. We suggest a travel blazer; you’re already shelling out a lot of money for flights and accommodations, so you can save a few bucks by not checking a full suit. Our style director, Christian Gollayan, recently did a full review of the Bonobos Jetsetter Knit Blazer. He described it as a “lifesaver” when traveling. You can definitely rock it at a fall destination wedding, especially considering the hardworking knit construction. For a lighter, beachy vibe, Buck Mason’s Capitola Linen Carry-On Jacket is my own go-to. It holds its shape well for linen, and some of the darker colors work well for any season.

Pants are easy to pack, so we’d suggest going with something that helps you stand out. The Bonobos Stretch Weekday Warrior Dress Pants are the perfect counterpart to the Jetsetter, and you can wear them around the office when you’re not in wedding mode. The Italian Linen Sutton Trousers are a luxury pick, and the white colorway pairs particularly well with a navy blazer for a classic look. They’re also a lot easier to pack than regular dress pants. If the destination wedding is beach-themed, you can even get away with rocking a tee underneath your blazer. You don’t want to go with something too casual, and the Heavyweight Jersey OG T-Shirt from Reigning Champ is anything but. It’s well-made, fits like a glove, and is a great way to show off some jewelry if you like to wear a chain or two.

#4873. The 6 Best On Shoes for Walking of 2026, Tested By Fitness Editors and Podiatrists

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a Women’s Health style writer, I regularly test the latest releases from all the major sneaker brands. On kicks are some of my favorites, and our editors and A-list celebs love ‘em too (including Zendaya). The Swiss brand has seen impressive growth over the past year, becoming a major competitor among sneaker giants like Nike and Adidas. On’s signature CloudTec cushioning not only makes you feel like you’re “walking on clouds,” but it’s also right on trend and a major style statement for wellness girlies.

We've named these kicks some of the best running shoes for plantar fasciitis, but after vigorous testing, we absolutely love On shoes for walking, too. Podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, says he walks around the city daily in his On sneakers because they make him feel supported and comfortable and accommodate his Dr. Scholl's insoles. "Thanks to the thicker sole and rounded heel, they provide that perfect mix of function, stability, and cushion without sacrificing any category," he says.

On has a large roster of comfortable sneakers, so it can be tricky to know where to start to find the perfect pair. That's why we tapped Schaeffer, podiatrist Daniel Geller, DPM, and Women's Health fitness editors to give us the lowdown on what to look for when shopping for the best On Cloud shoes for walking: in this case, weight, cushion, stability, and heel-to-toe drop.

Keep reading to see our favorites, and be sure to check out our 4-Week Walking Plan for the perfect workout to break in your new kicks.

After testing several pairs of On shoes, the Cloudrunner 3—a cushier, more supportive upgrade from the Cloudrunner 2—takes the top spot for a few key reasons. Executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos has tested more than a dozen On shoes and says the Cloudrunner 3 has become a go-to in her sneaker collection lately. That’s because the shoe has a relatively lightweight feel with tons of stability.

That balance comes from the sole, which is made with On’s Helion Superfoam. This material, made from thermoplastic polyurethane, blends firm and flexible foam components to create a lightweight, responsive, and well-cushioned feel. The mix of stiffer and softer sections absorbs impact from every step and actually helps propel you forward. The Cloudrunner 3 is actually a touch heavier than its predecessor (by only 0.7 ounces), but we chalk it up to the upgraded plush heel collar and wider base that offer a bit more comfort and stability. I’ve noticed this shoe is super durable, holding up to months of wear and tear on city sidewalks. During my walks in this shoe, I appreciate that I don’t feel overly bouncy, but the cushioning is still noticeable and light enough to help me feel grounded.“At nine months pregnant, I need to prioritize stability and comfort over everything else in a sneaker right now, and the On Cloudrunner 3s delivered for me,” Andriakos says. “It feels firm and supportive (and not overly cushioned), which has noticeably reduced my pelvic and low back pain when I’m on my feet all day and walking a lot.” She’s also been wearing it for hybrid strength-and-cardio workouts, and while it’s not a super-flat traditional lifting shoe, the fairly neutral sole and structured shape and feel make it surprisingly versatile. “Plus, the toe box is on the wider side and roomy enough for my swollen feet, so my toes can actually breathe,” Andriakos adds.

After about four months of testing an alarming amount of shoes, the On Cloudtilt Remix is my everyday go-to. That’s because this sneaker takes everything we love about the original Cloudtilt and gives it a fashion-forward upgrade with a techy upper designed with “X-ray layers,” or semi-transparent mesh overlays that look super sleek.

This shoe is basically built for walking, too, thanks to the CloudTec Phase midsole, a walking-focused cushioning system designed so each “cloud” compresses in sequence, delivering a smooth, plush ride. The result is an exceptionally smooth heel-to-toe transition that feels natural and effortless during long days on your feet. It also has a moderate 7 mm heel-to-toe drop, meaning it distributes weight evenly throughout the lower body and helps keep the foot in a neutral walking position, making it a pretty universal pick.

Underfoot, the cushioning lands squarely in the Goldilocks zone. The Helion superfoam provides plenty of impact absorption, but the ride never feels overly soft or marshmallow-like. Instead, it delivers a lightly responsive, cushioned feel that keeps your feet comfortable during long walks, travel days, and hours of sightseeing without sacrificing ground feel or stability. Lightweight, stylish, and genuinely built for all-day movement, the Cloudtilt Remix is the On sneaker I reach for when I want my shoes to work as hard as the rest of my outfit. The sleek, streamlined look is super easy to style with everything from tennis skirts to joggers to track pants. If you ask me, it’s kinda the perfect shoe that combines everything on this list into one sleek kick.

My one note is that I worry about the layered mesh upper being difficult to clean if the shoe gets too dirty. Luckily, I’ve managed to keep it pretty clean, but I avoid wearing this shoe in wet weather or otherwise messy conditions.

Hate tying your shoes? The Cloudnova Form 2 might be your new favorite—thanks to its easy slip-on, slip-off design, which Andriakos swears by. That said, it still has laces if you want to tighten things up for a more secure fit. This is my everyday shoe when I’m heading out the door to run errands or pop out for a walk but don’t feel like wearing anything bulky or something that needs a full lace adjustment (just lazy girl things!). It looks super cute with sweatpants and leggings, and a boxy t-shirt on top.

Comfort-wise, the Cloudnova Form is a win right out of the box. During my testing, I found that there was no break-in period needed (big ups). The moderately-cushioned sole is super balanced, which makes it ideal for long walks and power strolls, and Andriakos especially likes that it doesn’t have the super-prominent “bubble” look that many On shoes are known for. Instead, it has a lower-cut silhouette that feels a bit more grounded and less bouncy.

Another plus: The Form 2 is made with a breathable mesh upper and a soft microfiber tongue, so your feet stay cool and comfortable even on warm or extra-active days. On the downside, it runs small, so it’s a good idea to size it up by half. Also worth noting: it has a high heel-to-toe drop (14 mm), which can put extra stress on the knees and hips. If you deal with pain in those areas, you might want to skip this one.

On only offers wide sizing for certain models, but this shoe has a spacious toe box for a roomy fit. Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi has bunions and never experiences pain when wearing it. “Most sneakers that don’t come in wide sizing tend to irritate and rub against my bunions, which makes them throb, but not the Cloudmonster,” she says. “The toe box is surprisingly a perfect fit and lets me walk around for hours pain-free.”

This new version of the shoe delivers a cradling sensation while the foam slightly compresses to conform to your feet. The sensation is pillow-like under the foot while also offering a stable feel. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton notes that it's her all-time fave On walking shoe for its high-stack cushion, meaning it has a very thick foam between your foot and the ground. The 3 gets back to the Cloudmonster’s roots and becomes a good running shoe for intermediate to advanced runners again. That’s thanks to a speedboard that promotes a forward rolling motion, along with the aforementioned maxed cushioning. This has added only a little weight from the last model (6.6 ounces to 8.5), so you don’t have to worry about this shoe holding you back during long walks or runs.

"Whenever I want to feel super comfortable in my shoes but don't want that tight, locked-in feeling like I do when I'm running, the Cloudmonster is my go-to," Appleton says. She wore the shoe while moving into her fourth-floor Brooklyn walk-up, and notes it kept her feet comfortable all day. And while it’s great for getting your steps in, this shoe has that chunky look that’s super on trend right now. I love pairing it with tailored pants and a boxy t-shirt on top for that upgraded activewear vibe.

The heel-to-toe drop is also on the smaller side at six millimeters, which Accardi says distributes impact evenly on the knees, hips, and ankles. “As someone with knee issues, taking the load off my knees is essential, especially post-run,” she says. If you’re a heel striker and don’t struggle with pain in these areas, the Cloudrunner 2 could be a better fit.

If your workouts don’t fit neatly into one category, the On Cloud X 4 is the sneaker you’ll want on standby. Designed specifically for mixed training, it’s comfortable, responsive, and stable, making it equally suited for walking, HIIT training, and gym sessions. Unlike some of On’s chunkier models, the Cloud X 4 has a slightly lower-profile silhouette that looks and feels sleeker on foot, pairing easily with everyday outfits and activewear.

The shoe features On’s signature CloudTec cushioning, which delivers a comfortable, impact-absorbing ride without feeling overly squishy. Andriakos, who logs a high daily step count, says it’s become one of her favorite shoes for long walks because the cushioning feels nice and plush while maintaining a grounded feel. “The mesh upper is super breathable, so my feet don’t feel overheated and sweaty after long walks, and small design details (like the cool X lace pattern from above!) make it feel really polished,” she says.

The supportive lacing system creates a secure, locked-in feel that feels stable during lateral movements and dynamic workouts. “I’ve worn it to HIIT classes, and it feels super supportive, though I’d still opt for a flatter, more structured shoe for traditional lifting,” Andriakos says. The mesh upper is a nice touch, too, keeping things super breathable so your feet don’t get overheated or sweaty on long walks.

The On Cloud 6 Coast is a refreshed take on the brand’s classic On Cloud—but this ultra-lightweight version takes it even further. It keeps all the upgrades of the latest model, including the original slip-on, no-lace design and On’s signature CloudTec cushioning system. The big win here? It weighs in at just 6.5 ounces. That means your ultra-cushioned shoe is now perfect for traveling, long days on your feet, or hot, humid commutes. It’s built with an updated mesh that’s super breathable and ventilated—you can even wear this shoe barefoot!It also features a wider opening for a more inclusive, easy-on fit. I really appreciated this feature as a wide-footed girly. It also has a moderate heel-to-toe drop of 8 mm, making it a great universal walking shoe. Bottom line: this shoe is made to handle just about anything, which makes it a must-have in your rotation.

This shoe has a medium cushion level for that sweet spot that’s comfortable and light on your feet without being overly plush. The CloudTec midsole does a great job absorbing impact, making it a solid choice for everything from sightseeing and airport sprints to casual daily walks. The lightweight build almost disappears on your foot, which is exactly what you want when you’re packing light or spending hours exploring.

The tradeoff for all that packability and featherlight comfort is support. The flexible upper and minimalist construction can feel a bit flimsy compared to more structured walking shoes, especially if you need extra arch support or stability.

On sneakers are extremely comfortable, but Schaeffer says that's because most of its shoes have a bit of weight to them. If a shoe is too lightweight (under four ounces), it sacrifices function and stability, he says. But, don't get it twisted—these don't feel like bricks on your feet either. Most On shoes are between four and 10 ounces, which means they're the perfect medium weight that doesn’t slack on support.

A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer says to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Support and stability are the number one qualities you should look for in a walking shoe, says Geller. He notes that when arches are supported, you create an "excellent" platform to launch from, meaning the feet are in the ideal position for takeoff and landing. This can help avoid foot injuries down the line.

Geller also says that many good walking shoes, including motion control shoes, will have medial posting—a firm wedge in the arch that holds up the heel—and firm cushioning for more support. "Firmer cushioning will resist the inward roll of the foot [overpronation], controlling the knees and hips better," he says.

If stability is a priority for you, also consider shoes with a broader sole to minimize excess movement. The increased material along the sides and front of your foot creates a wider platform, which is naturally resistant to feet rolling or wobbling, says Geller. In other words, it's a great feature for walkers who overpronate.

"Whenever you’re looking for a good walking shoe, you want to find a great mix of comfort and stability," says Schaeffer. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but the level of cushioning will vary depending on your specific foot needs.

Wearing running shoes for walking isn’t inherently bad, but it’s not always the best idea either. Shoes designed specifically for running tend to have significantly more cushioning to absorb the higher impact that comes with each stride. “This isn't necessary for walking and reduces your feel of the ground, which is problematic for those with any balance issues or previous falls," Milica McDowell, a doctor of physical therapy, previously told Women’s Health.

Running shoes often have a very tight fit for higher performance, a narrow toe box, or are highly supported in the arch, which are features a lifestyle walker does not need, says McDowell. That’s why, in most cases, walkers are recommended to opt for a shoe designed specifically for walking (or one labeled for walking and running).

To curate a list of the best On walking shoes, I tested On kicks for two years, alongside fitness contributor Talene Appleton, NASM-CPT, fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, style contributor Lily Wohlner, and executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos.

We wore them during long and short walks for at least several hours at a time. We evaluated each shoe based on:

He signed a record-breaking contract with the Cincinnati Bengals in 2023, but where does Joe Burrow live when he’s not on the field?

The NFL quarterback was born in Ames, Iowa, in 1996. His family moved to Ohio when he was eight, and he has resided mostly in the Buckeye State ever since. Three years later Burrow signed a $275 million five-year extension, making him the highest-paid player in NFL history at the time, according to ESPN.

It’s unsurprising, then, that Burrow has put down roots in the Buckeye State. Below, we’re examining the quarterback’s real estate portfolio.

In May 2020, a month after being selected first overall in the NFL Draft, Burrow revealed that he was spending the pandemic lockdown in his old bedroom at his parents’ house in The Plains, Ohio, just outside of Athens. Interior design apparently wasn’t at the forefront of his mind; the room still had his childhood Star Wars curtains and posters on the wall, though he had given the bed a king-size upgrade in high school, replacing the Star Wars comforter that once rounded out the room’s theme. #4870. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4868. The Six Bells Madewell Collection 2026

Whimsical design flourishes, cozy interiors, and close proximity to upstate antiquing all make The Six Bells Countryside Inn one of the best weekend escapes in the Empire State. Now, thanks to Madewell, you never have to check out. Launching today, the two brands have joined forces on a 28-piece holiday capsule of heirloom-worthy wardrobe and home essentials inspired by The Six Bells’ vintage aesthetic. Pieces specifically pay homage to the hotel’s interiors through references to archival patterns and wallpaper prints found throughout the Inn’s rooms and communal spaces.

“We fell in love with [The Six Bells’] distinct, whimsical world—the mix of patterns, the nostalgic sentiment, and the personality in every detail,” says Madewell creative director Steven Cateron. During initial planning for the clothing brand’s holiday collection, the Rosendale, New York-based hotel became an unexpected source of inspiration for Cateron and his team because of the shared appreciation for heritage and storytelling. “Each piece has intention, whether it’s to wear day-to-day or for a celebration, a gifting moment for a loved one or hostess, or pajama pieces that lean into cozy season,” he says.

Sock slippers from the collaboration and Madewell’s classic denim make a perfect pairing.

Founded by Audrey Gelman in 2025, who designed the hotel in collaboration with interiors firm GrecoDeco, the Countryside Inn has quickly risen in popularity—even earning a spot in AD’s list of Great Design Hotels last year. “This project is so rooted in a shared love of the decorative arts and global human history,” designer Adam Greco previously told AD. Design-wise, maximalism dominates the interiors. Picture: rooms wrapped in fretwork wallpaper and deep cinnabar paint, with pistachio window shades and striped seating.

The collection also builds on the fantasy of Barrow’s Green, the fictional English village dreamed up by Gelman that includes its own imaginary landmarks and distinct locals (including a town gossip and poignant editor). “It was so interesting to broaden our fimaginations and think about how The Six Bells’ style could be brought to life through clothes,” says Gelman.

A cheeky message makes this classic needlepoint pillow pop.

At the same time, the collaboration was an opportunity to venture into Madwell’s less-explored categories—specifically the home space. The collection’s interior goods are a practice in curated nostalgia: There are holiday ornaments you’ll reach for year after year, scented candles and soaps to integrate into your daily winter routine, and cozy pajamas inspired by vintage sleep silhouettes. “If it’s something we don’t currently offer, we want to work with people that do the category best,” says Cateron. “The Six Bells team were the perfect partners to bring this collection’s home accessories to life.”

Still, versatility isn’t lost in the assortment. In designing the clothing, Cateron made sure to include “pieces to wear upstate, in the city, or for day-to-day celebrations.” Classic denim jackets are neutral staples that you can reach for any day of the week, while fair-isle wool knits are seasonally appropriate while still feeling adaptable enough to wear after the holidays. “There’s a real point of view behind every detail [at the Countryside Inn], from the interiors to collected vintage pieces,” says Cateron. “This collection captures that sensibility in a way that felt authentic to both brands.”

The collection is available to shop on Madewell.com and in Madewell stores starting today, November 12.

“There’s so much character in every detail at The Six Bells, and we wanted to bring that sensibility into each piece,” says Madewell creative director Steven Cateron.

#4866. Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

Being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

While MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” said Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

New diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise important questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also important to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder said.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

“No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

“MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder said. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research shows females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several important changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

The revised criteria also include new MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

If you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

“A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder said.

#4865. Nickey Kehoe’s New Collection With The Lacquer Company Takes Its Cues From Beloved Antiques

In 2024, AD heralded the return of lacquer. In our April 2026 issue, cover star Athena Calderone was pictured leaning over an enormous burgundy-lacquered kitchen island, and in May, cover star Mark Grattan showed off his parrot green lacquer walls. Today’s collaboration between AD100 design firm Nickey Kehoe and The Lacquer Company brings the glossy finish down to a slightly more manageable scale, applying it to coffee tables, desks, trays, and tissue boxes. Nickey Kehoe founders Todd Nickey and Amy Kehoe designed the 30-piece collection with The Lacquer Company founder James Lowther, drawing on antique furniture and objects the three have collected over the years.

The Bonne Nuit nightstand in Cassis staged among various Nickey Kehoe textiles and an upholstered headboard.

The Florin Tray in Carreaux & Marine Blue is styled with all small pieces from the Nickey Kehoe collection.

Many of the pieces, as is often true of Nickey Kehoe’s in-house catalog, draw on the founders’ personal vintage collections. The Pastis side table is based on a bamboo folding table that belongs to Nickey. The Hugo desk is a Louis XVI–style writing desk, with tapered, fluted legs, brass details, and three soft-close drawers in a bright red lacquer. The colorways sound like a very civilized, French late lunch: cassis and lettuce green, carreaux and marine blue, khaki and chocolate brown. The Jules catchall tray comes with a matching tissue box cover for the powder room.

Lacquer trays, tissue boxes, side tables, and the collection’s coffee table are staged together here to show the full line.

The Pastis side table references a vintage style with the lacquer and bamboo combination reminiscent of Regency Chinoiserie.

Lowther bought his first piece of lacquer, a burnt-orange betel box, while traveling in Burma in 1999, and it’s still one of his favorite things. He later found the craftspeople he was looking for in Saigon, and every piece from The Lacquer Company is still made there in Sơn Mài lacquer, a Vietnamese art form that goes back centuries. The process is lengthy: Wood is first sealed with a resin called Sinh. It’s then coated repeatedly with natural lacquer mixed with ground mountain rock, alluvial soil, and cashew nut shell oil. Each coat is wet-sanded until it’s smooth before the next coat is applied. “There is no prescribed drying time, no set number of layers,” according to the company. That makes the eight- to 12-week lead time on larger pieces easier to forgive.

Nickey Kehoe’s goal is for its furniture to feel “as if it was acquired, not purchased.” With these pieces so rooted in vintage styles and techniques, they make good on their promise.

The collection is available to shop on NickeyKehoe.com.

#4863. RFK Jr.’s Revised Vaccine Schedule May Cause 83% Surge in Hepatitis B Infections

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers.

Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B.

A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommends individual-based clinical decision making.

After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary.

Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates.

“Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

“The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.”

Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team.

A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario.

With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination.

The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing.

Another study published in JAMA Pediatrics in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted.

However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors.

In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendation shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg).

Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old.

The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance.

However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines.

Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver.

Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults.

Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B.

“We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said.

Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer.

“The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said.

Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection.

“Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said.

“The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.”

In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy.

The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates.

The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data.

Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases.

Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional.

“Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said.

“Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.”

While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections.

Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series.

You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection.

An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby.

“I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said.

“There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said.

#4861. How One Designer Brought a Discerning Eye to Her Deeply Personal Manhattan Apartment

Ask an interior designer about their most difficult client, and there’s a good chance they’ll name themselves. Dani Dennis spent more than a decade at Mark Cunningham Inc. before founding her own New York–based practice, Danielette Dennis Interiors, translating other people’s tastes into rooms. “I’m such a decisive person,” she says of her approach to projects ranging from a traditional Brooklyn Heights townhouse to a sleek Park Avenue pied-à-terre. But when it came to decorating her own Gramercy Park apartment that she shares with her husband and two daughters, Dennis had no client brief to answer to—and no one to make the final call but herself.

When the family moved in three years ago, the apartment had plenty going for it: tall windows, handsome moldings, and an airy living and dining area. Dennis left the architecture alone, putting furniture, textiles, and her growing art collection to work instead. Benjamin Moore’s Steam keeps the walls a warm white, though the rooms are anything but hands-off. “I almost wanted it to feel like a gallery,” she says. “But, obviously, it’s lived in, and I have kids, so nothing is too precious.”

A portrait by Patrick Eugène, sourced via Mariane Ibrahim, anchors one end of the living room. Nearby are an Alfred Grenander chair upholstered in Toyine Sellers fabric, a black mushroom side table by Emma Donnersberg, and Christian Woo’s Noga Cube side table.

A portrait of a young girl by Jerrell Gibbs hangs near a Pierre Augustin Rose Cadillac ottoman upholstered in Rosemary Hallgarten’s alpaca bouclé. Vintage Saint-Louis crystal, sourced at the Paris flea market, sits atop the credenza.

The living room’s opposing sofas encourage conversation. The sofa (right), upholstered in Pierre Frey wool and mohair, is by Marked NYC. The ceiling fixture is a reedition of Pierre Chareau’s Quart de Rond lamp, and the rug is by Scott Group Studio.

Joseph-André Motte chairs surround the dining table, while a 1960s Italian burlwood credenza from Naga Antiques sits beneath an abstract painting by Carmen Neely. The dining rug is by Crosby Street Studios.

A first-generation American of Liberian heritage, Dennis has built a collection of art that includes contemporary Black artists from across the diaspora. A painting of girls playing in a circle takes her back to her school days in Côte d’Ivoire. Others show Black women in moments of rest and repose. “I want my kids and my family to be surrounded by reflections of us,” she says. Her clients’ collections tell their own stories; this one tells hers. Black joy runs through the collection, but Dennis doesn’t shop by theme; she listens to her gut. “I buy what I love,” she says. “I don’t buy for decoration.”

Dennis is equally at ease with an English-country chintz and a graphic geometric. In her own home, she borrows a little from everywhere, favoring clean lines and unexpected combinations. A custom sofa in Sanderson velvet faces a curved Marked NYC design in Pierre Frey wool and mohair. Camel-colored lounge chairs play against the sharp geometry of a Roger Sprunger coffee table; a 1906 Josef Hoffmann side table and an early-20th-century Alfred Grenander chair join the mix. “When the harmony comes from shape and proportion and feeling, I think that’s what makes spaces dynamic,” she says.

An expressive Ferrari Sheppard painting, acquired through Massimo De Carlo in Milan, hangs above a custom sofa upholstered in Sanderson’s indigo Quartz velvet. Camel-colored chairs wear Holland & Sherry fabric. A glass-and-metal coffee table by Roger Sprunger joins a modernist stool by Charles Vandenhove and JM Szymanski’s slender Table No. 3.

Dennis took a moodier approach in the library, where the family gathers. The walls and ceiling are painted the same dark hue, creating a cozy retreat for her two daughters, who prefer sprawling on the soft rug to sitting on the sofa. Artwork includes a floral painting by Alexandria Tarver and Hazel Mphande’s Stone or Lavender (2021). The striped pillows are in Fortuny fabric.

The dining table seats 10. Dinner guests, however, are still forthcoming. “I haven't had people over yet, because in my head it’s not done,” Dennis says. Joseph-André Motte chairs surround the table, while a 1960s Italian burlwood credenza and a Crosby Street Studios rug anchor the dining area. The living room sofas were positioned for entertaining too, although the family’s day-to-day use of the space is less formal. For Dennis’s daughters, 10 and seven, the mohair-and-wool sofa comes with ground rules: “You guys can sit on it, you can perch, but if we want to play, let’s do it elsewhere.”

The library, on the other hand, is fair game. The girls can sprawl out with a book or watch TV, though they rarely bother with the sofa. “They’re always lying on the rug,” Dennis says. She painted the walls a deep olive-green, carrying it across the ceiling for an enveloping effect. The art also takes a moodier turn, with a floral painting by Alexandria Tarver and a black-and-white self-portrait by Hazel Mphande. The primary bedroom, meanwhile, provides a brighter, quieter escape. “I always wanted to be in a cloud,” the designer says of the neutral palette. The upholstered bed, 1970s steel bench in alpaca wool, and leather-bound nightstands supply the texture.

Since the photo shoot, Dennis has switched out accessories and rearranged objects. When she recently swapped a lamp in the living room, even her husband took notice. “Another one?” he asked. At work, Dennis knows when to call a room finished. At home, she’s beginning to wonder why she should.

“I always wanted to be in a cloud,” Dennis says of the primary bedroom, where texture takes precedence over color. A vintage 1970s steel bench with alpaca upholstery sits at the foot of the bed, while leather-clad nightstands add another tactile element. The ceramic lamp is by Christiane Perrochon, and the understated artwork above the bed is by Carmen Neely.

#4860. Functional Core Workouts Are the Key to Moving Better in and Out of the Gym

Add these 15 expert-approved exercises into your weekly routine.

I don’t know about you, but doing core exercises is my least favorite part of workouts. Unfortunately, though, neglecting functional core training can make a big difference in your total-body strength, and how you move day to day.

Functional training focuses on compound movements that engage multiple muscle groups simultaneously and mimic the way our bodies move during everyday activities. Functionally training the core, specifically, involves strengthening the abdominal muscles that attach to the pelvis or spine.

For instance, a farmer’s carry mirrors the movement of carrying grocery bags. “This is an example of ‘bracing and carrying,’ where you need to keep a tight, braced core to carry the heavy weight,” says Corrine Carnation, CPT, a personal and group trainer at Equinox and creator of the Better You, Better Living program. Plus, a weak core can lead to poor posture and an increased risk of injury.

But the benefits extend way beyond preparing your body for real-life activities and protecting against pain or injury—keep reading for all the reasons you should do functional core movements.

Meet the experts: Corrine Carnation, CPT, is a personal and group trainer at Equinox. Cori Ritchey, CSCS, is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and conditioning coach and group fitness instructor in New York City.

Time: 30 minutes | Equipment (optional): kettlebell, dumbbells, slam ball, resistance band, or Pilates ring | Good for: core, hips, back

Instructions: Choose 5 to 6 exercises from the list below. Complete 2 to 3 sets of the indicated number of reps for each move. Aim to integrate functional core exercises into your training routine once or twice a week.

As these exercises become easier with practice, challenge yourself by increasing resistance while slightly decreasing the number of reps. For example, if 3 sets of 10 reps using bodyweight alone feels easy, try adding a weight or resistance band for 2 or 3 sets of 8 reps. By the last rep of each set, you should feel ready to stop but not completely at failure. When in doubt, start with bodyweight only, then add resistance until you feel the exercise is challenging, but doable.

Pro tip: Exercises aren’t one-size-fits-all, so it’s important to recognize when an exercise is either too challenging, too easy, or not comfortable for you. Keep in mind that every exercise can be modified if needed!

Why it rocks: The suitcase carry prepares the core for real-life activities such as carrying heavy things by your sides. It strengthens the core by making you resist the urge to bend, improving stability and balance—the added grip demand is a fun challenge, too.

1. Holding a weight in one hand, stand up tall and pull your shoulders back and down to prevent them from rolling forward. Keep your core tight and spine neutral.

2. Walk forward for 30 to 60 seconds while maintaining a strong grip and upright posture.

4. Turn around and pick the weight up again, this time with your left hand. Complete 4 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The halo exercise improves shoulder mobility and stability while strengthening your core. Moving the weight around your head causes a perturbation (or distracting force) to your body, forcing you to stabilize using your core. This particular halo variation has the added benefit of enhancing upper-body strength, targeting the shoulders, back, and arms.

1. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding one dumbbell in front of your chest with both hands and elbows bent at 90 degrees.

2. Slowly circle the dumbbell around your head, moving it clockwise from ear to ear, elbows hugging in.

3. Return to start and repeat the movement counterclockwise. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Have you ever worried about straining your back when picking something up or twisting? This move strengthens the core, improves stability, and builds rotational strength to protect your body during these movements.

1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and upper body leaned back until abs are engaged (aim for a 45-degree angle relative to the floor). Hold a slam ball or dumbbell close to your chest with your elbows bent.

2. Keeping your arms slightly bent, twist your torso to the left and slam the ball on the floor next to your left hip.

3. Twist your torso through center to the right and slam the ball on the floor near your right hip. That's 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating for a total of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: The overhead slam exercise requires you to stabilize your body as you lift and forcefully throw the ball down to the floor. It also strengthens your shoulders, arms, and upper back while improving explosive power and coordination.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, a soft bend in knees, and core engaged, while holding a slam ball at your chest with both hands.

2. Rise up tall on your toes and extend your arms overhead holding the slam ball.

3. Bend at your hips (hinging forward slightly) and slam the ball on the floor directly in front of you. Exhale as you throw the ball down toward the floor with force. Be careful not to arch your back.

4. Catch the ball on the bounce while lowering back into the squat position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: The wood chop exercise helps strengthen your core by working your abs and obliques, which can boost your twisting power and stability, building strength and coordination.

1. Start in a half-kneeling position with your left leg forward and your right leg back, both bent at 90 degrees, holding a dumbbell in front of your chest.

2. With your arms straight, torso upright, and hips facing forward, swiftly lower the weight diagonally across your body to the right hip while twisting to the right. Then, raise the weight to upper left diagonal while twisting to the left. That's 1 rep.

3. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on the other side.

Why it rocks: Keeping your lower back and head flush with the floor while your limbs shift weight will engage your deep core stabilizers. Being able to lift your legs and arms from this position is essential for a healthy spine.

1. Lie faceup holding one dumbbell horizontally in front of your chest with both hands. Lift legs to a tabletop position with your knees over hips, your lower back glued to the floor, and your core engaged.

2. Keeping one leg at a 90-degree angle, lower the other to tap your heel to the floor. As your leg lowers, reach your arms above your head to lower the weight toward the floor behind your head.

3. Engage your core to lift both your arms and leg back to start, then repeat on the opposite side. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise recruits your abdominal muscles to maintain balance and stability. A resistance band offers an added challenge for the core and lower body.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart and your hands on your hips or relaxed at your sides. (Optional: Place a resistance band around the arches of both feet.)

2. Balancing on one leg, draw one knee up toward your chest, hold for 1 second, then return it to the floor.

3. Repeat on the opposite side, alternating for 30 seconds. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: Planks help you build the strength to push yourself up from the floor, which is important for many day-to-day activities. Adding the knee drive challenges your upper body and core to stabilize, improving your balance and coordination with uneven movements.

1. Start in a high plank position with your right foot lifted slightly up off the floor.

2. Exhale and pull your right knee toward your chest while rounding the spine to bring your nose toward your knee.

3. With control, reverse movement to return to plank position with right foot lifted. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise challenges you to sit up and lie down without using your hands, which requires strong core muscles. You can do it with a Pilates ring, a ball, or no equipment at all.

1. Lie faceup with your legs slightly bent, heels on floor, and arms extended straight above your head. (Optional: Place a mini resistance band around your wrists for an added challenge.)

2. Engage your core and draw your belly button in as you slowly begin to curl your spine off the mat one vertebra at a time. Roll up to an upright seated position while keeping biceps by the ears and arms reaching to the ceiling.

3. Once you reach the upright position, gradually reverse the movement by slowly rolling back down to the lying position. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: This exercise targets the glutes and core, the muscles needed to lift your hips. It's great for anyone who sits a lot, as it both strengthens and mobilizes the hips.

1. Lie faceup with knees bent and feet planted shoulder-width apart on the floor. Place your arms on the floor by your sides or for an added challenge, extend arms above with your hands directly above your shoulders and your palms facing in.

2. Engage your core as you press up into a glute bridge with your knees, hips, and shoulders in alignment, and hold this position.

3. From here, raise your right leg to a 90-degree angle, keeping the stationary leg firmly on the floor and pelvis stable. Return right foot to meet left foot in starting position. That’s 1 rep.

4. Continue alternating legs with your butt lifted and complete 10 to 12 reps on each side.

Why it rocks: The classic side plank targets the obliques, which are essential for stability and rotation in daily activities. It also works your shoulders and hips, promoting good posture and alignment.

1. Lie on your right side with your legs bent, your right elbow directly under your shoulder, and your left hand palm down.

2. Lift your hips off the mat, extending your legs to form a straight line from your head to heels.

3. Hold the position for 30 seconds, then repeat on the opposite side. That’s 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's similar to the suitcase carry, but levels up the move a bit by testing your stabilization, as you have to stay upright even though the weight is trying to pull you down. Plus, it boosts your grip strength.

1. Stand up straight with feet shoulder-width apart and dumbbell in left hand.

2. Extend your right arm out to the side at a 45-degree angle from your body.

3. Slowly lift your left leg up until knee is at hip height.

4. Then, with control, lower your leg down to the floor. Repeat with right leg. That's 1 rep.

5. Complete 10 to 12 reps, then switch the dumbbell to your right hand.

Why it rocks: It targets your obliques, but also challenges your other core muscles in a more uncommon position. Additionally, it works your spinal mobility.

1. Kneel on left knee with toes pointed to the right, and right foot planted firmly to the side of body, holding a kettlebell in right hand.

2. Rack the kettlebell at chest, then lift it overhead, keeping eyes on the weight.

3. Slowly lower body down until left hand reaches the floor, then continue lowering until elbow and forearm reach the floor.

4. Reverse the movement with control and return to start. That's 1 rep.

Why it rocks: It's important to train rotation because we're constantly rotating in real life. Plank hip dips strengthen the obliques and stabilize the spine.

1. Start in a forearm plank position with elbows under shoulders and knees, hips, and torso in a straight line.

2. Drop right hip toward the floor, then return to center.

3. Immediately drop the left hip toward the floor.

Why it rocks: This move is one of the best for training functional power, and it demands stabilization from your core.

1. Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width apart. Hold a kettlebell in front of your body with both hands, arms straight.

2. With a slight bend in the knees and a flat back, hinge at the hips and swing the kettlebell back through the legs. Use that momentum to stand and swing the kettlebell out in front of your body, up to shoulder height.

3. Thrust the hips forward and engage the glutes and core as you stand up straight. When the kettlebell hits shoulder height, the knees should be straight and glutes contracted in a full hip extension.

4. Allow the kettlebell to swing back down through the legs, while hinging at the hips. That's 1 rep.

The best functional core workouts include bodyweight and resistance exercises that challenge the core in different positions and directions. Your core is not one-dimensional, so it’s important to strengthen your body through movements that involve twisting, bending, and stabilizing in all directions. For example, a traditional situp only engages the core in a single plane of motion, but a workout with a Russian twist (for rotational movement), lateral side bends (for side-to-side movement), and plank variations (for multidirectional stability) ensures you are hitting your core muscles from all angles.

Carnation notes the importance of first activating your core before jumping right into a workout. To do so, she recommends the following: “Act as if someone is about to throw a basketball at your stomach.” It might sound odd, but this cue can be really effective in helping you tighten and brace your core to get ready for impact. It’s best to practice this abdominal bracing technique before going into more advanced exercises in order to ensure your core is engaged and ready for action, Carnation says.

Rachel Tavel is a doctor of physical therapy, strength and conditioning specialist certified by the National Strength and Conditioning Association, and writer. Her writing has been published in Forbes, Fortune, Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Runner’s World, SELF, Bicycling Magazine, The Huffington Post, and more. She co-authored the book “Stretch Yourself Healthy Guide: Easy Routines to Relieve Pain, Boost Energy, and Feel Refreshed” (Prevention, 2020) and is a Forbes Health Advisory Board Member. Prior to becoming a physical therapist, Rachel was a travel writer living and traveling throughout South America. Connect: www.racheltavel.com, @racheltaveldpt, Email: hello@racheltavel.com.

#4858. 7 Best Cheese Boards for Entertaining Centerpieces (2026)

The calendar pointing toward the holidays also means that cheese board season is here. The platters function as a key part of any festive gathering, serving as the meeting point for people to nibble and mingle before they take a seat. But it’s much more than a way to display finger foods. Often situated in a central location at a party, a cheese board works as a decorative design piece, and when done well, can even be a conversation starter. In fact, some boards themselves read as a still life, even after half the Brie is gone.

The most unique cheese boards combine material and shape, offering something distinct and memorable to house the bites (or function as a surface for slicing a baguette). Simplicity is often best with creatine. Look for products that list creatine as the sole active ingredient, ideally without added sugars, unless you're choosing a flavored version intentionally. Avoid proprietary blends that don’t disclose exact creatine content per serving.

The recommended daily dose of creatine is a minimum of five grams per day, according to the International Society of Sports Nutrition. This amount is shown to be safe and effective for maintaining creatine saturation within the muscles.
