#4856. Emideltide Keeps Getting a ‘No’ for Compounding. What’s the Problem?

Why the government’s renewed interest in peptides excludes this one.

THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION has not been shy about its pro-peptide stance. US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has pushed to make six popular yet unapproved peptides available for compounding to people with a prescription. A recent FDA advisory committee meeting voted in favor of adding six out of seven peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply.

Six out of seven. So what happened to that last peptide? Emideltide, also dubbed DSIP, is a peptide people have turned to for better sleep. And it was the only peptide the FDA advisory board voted against moving out of the Category 2 list—a substance considered to carry significant safety risks, with compounding pharmacies prohibited from making it. Here’s why.

EMIDELTIDE IS A nine-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits during electrically induced sleep in the late 1970s. Since its discovery, a synthetic peptide version has been administered via injection or a nasal spray.

Emideltide reportedly helps you fall asleep faster and extend the time spent in deep sleep. It’s also been used to avoid waking up multiple times throughout the night and anecdotal reports online have mentioned more vivid, Inception–like lucid dreaming. With better sleep, people online using emideltide have mentioned feeling less stress, more refreshed upon waking, and faster recovery after a grueling workout.

MOST RESEARCH LOOKING into the peptide’s role in sleep, however, took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed findings.

For example, a 1984 case study reported on a 35-year-old guy with 10 years of narcolepsy who had reduced sleep attacks, less daytime napping, and more alertness with weekly emideltide injections administered in the morning.

One clinical trial had 16 people take an emideltide injection or a placebo while measuring how long it took for them to fall asleep once they’re tucked into bed. People who had an emideltide injection said they felt more tired and actually went to sleep quicker than the placebo group. That should be great except when they repeated the experiment a second night, the placebo group knocked out quicker than the peptide group.

Another study in 1992 found the peptide helped chronic insomniacs feel less tired. However, there was such little difference in the time it took to fall asleep and stay asleep in the emideltide group versus the placebo group. The authors of the 1992 study said any small improvements with the peptide were probably “due to an incidental change in the placebo group” and “not likely to be of major therapeutic benefit.”

BEYOND SLEEP, EMIDELTIDE has been explored in animal studies for potentially protecting against cancer and improving motor ability after stroke. Another realm of interest is how emideltide might help with curbing withdrawal after addiction.

A 1984 study found emideltide injections helped reduce the severity of opioid withdrawal symptoms in 97 percent of people with addiction along with alcohol withdrawal symptoms in 87 percent of people with alcohol addiction. Although more peptide injections were needed in people with opiate addiction.

In 1998, researchers gave a single injection of emideltide to seven people with opioid dependence. While they reported improvements in opioid withdrawal, the team also noted “it remains an open question whether DSIP could be an effective alternative detoxification approach.” Some of the issues were the small sample size, lack of a placebo group for proper comparison, and that each person knew they were getting an emideltide injection. The lack of randomization makes it hard to say for sure that a treatment actually worked or if people subjectively felt better because they knew they were getting treatment.

WE KNOW EMIDELTIDE doesn’t act like a sedative that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

The peptide is often considered a sleep-regulator rather than a suppressant. We know emideltide doesn’t act like a sedative or sleeping pill that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

One possible mechanism is that the peptide increases delta-wave activity. These are your slowest brain waves at 0.5 to 4 Hz that are indicative of deep sleep. Deep sleep is linked to better memory, energy, and all that good stuff you get from a good night’s sleep. There may also be some neuroendocrine effects going on that could explain why people feel calm enough to pass out. A small study back in the ’80s injected a single dose of emideltide in 11 guys and found lower levels of ACTH, a hormone that stimulates your adrenal glands to release the stress hormone cortisol (though this mechanism has been disputed).

The FDA advisory meeting relied on studies that focused on emideltide’s cross-talk with the opioid system in the brain. While the peptide doesn’t directly interact with opioid receptors, evidence points to emideltide somehow being able to trigger the release of endorphins. This may also provide painkiller properties (which is why it’s been proposed as a way to suppress alcohol and opioid withdrawal syndrome).

EMIDELTIDE WILL PROBABLY stay banned—and found only through the sketchy gray market—because there’s not enough information to know if emideltide might do more harm than good.

Since emideltide interacts with the opioid system, there is a possibility that it could lead to addiction. Right now, there are no animal or human studies that prove emideltide wouldn’t worsen addictive behaviors.

There’s also not enough data on whether repeated emideltide use would cause other safety issues. While the small sleep trials did not report any serious side effects, withdrawal studies noted headaches, nausea, and vertigo. After the second injection, some had low blood pressure although the researchers also said it’s unclear whether those symptoms were because of the peptide or from withdrawal altogether.

Jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

#4855. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4853. Want Studio-Style Pilates at Home? Start With These Editor-Tested Reformers

Our top picks for every kind of at-home Pilates setup, from compact machines to studio-worthy reformers.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you’re a pilates princess, you already know what a reformer is, and you’re well acquainted with the many ways it delivers a low-impact, strength-building workout. However, if you’re a newbie, here’s a quick crash course: A reformer is a specially designed machine, originally developed by Joseph Pilates, that consists of springs for resistance, a moving carriage, a foot bar that you push or pull, and pulleys to hold onto or hook to your feet when performing pilates exercises.

“I’d describe the reformer as a machine designed to help create an understanding of your body with resistance,” says Sam Miles, owner and co-founder of Good Time Pilates in New York City. “It gives real time feedback so you can find sensation through the shortening and lengthening of your muscles. In short and easy terms: an assist to finding your muscle engagement!”

There are unique benefits to using a reformer that are hard to replicate in a pilates mat workout, or really any other type of workout. But that doesn’t mean you have to be advanced to start using one. “The modifications to increase or decrease challenge make it a truly universal machine for any body and any fitness level, which is very unique and just awesome,” Miles says. “You can rehabilitate with a reformer, strengthen muscles, stretch and find release work, it’s the best!”

Pilates reformers are available in different types: classical and contemporary. The classical reformer stays true to Joseph Pilates’ original design; the machines are made of wood, and have springs that all have the exact same resistance level. Purists are going to want to consider these machines.

Contemporary reformers are an evolutionary riff on the original and often incorporate springs of varying resistance that can be adjusted. The dimensions also usually vary a bit from the OG classical reformer design.

While it used to be that reformers were only found in Pilates studios, more and more women are investing in a reformer as an addition to their home gym setup. There are also less intense reformer models on the market that are specifically designed for at-home use, and these generally come in at a fraction of the cost of a classical or studio-grade contemporary reformer.

After testing a bunch of options, we narrowed down our picks to a variety of machines, including commercial-grade reformers and pared-down, reimagined reformers that are made specifically to take up less space and be more affordable.

After testing a handful of Pilates reformers, the contemporary-style Balanced Body Allegro 2 came out on top for its studio-quality, strong springs, durable build, and versatile foot bar. WH fitness contributor Talene Appleton has been using it two to three times a week to practice at home for almost two years, and it’s still in mint condition. Appleton says it’s built like a tank and is commercial-grade, so it’s the best you can get for your at-home gym setup.

Five springs are featured for varying tension to accommodate different levels—three high resistance (red), one medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow), while the steel, grippy foot bar glides effortlessly for 10 vertical and horizontal positions. “I was blown away by how much the additional positions of its foot bar allowed me to change up my usual Pilates sequences,” says Appleton. “This adds incredible versatility in terms of movement options that most competitors can’t beat.” While the foot bar is its best feature, Appleton notes it’s the most difficult to set up and requires two people to line it up evenly on each side.Appleton says this machine is best for advanced users, given there’s a bit of a learning curve at first. “Using a traditional reformer at home can be a bit overwhelming at first, especially if you’re used to having an instructor call the shots in terms of spring resistance, foot bar positions, moves, and all the rest,” she says. “I found myself second-guessing my setup and wondering if I was getting the most out of each exercise (or sometimes if the move I was doing was even a real exercise at all).” She credits YouTube and TikTok tutorials for guiding her along, specifically from Balanced Body and East River Pilates.While this is the best Pilates machine money can buy (with a steep price tag of $4,345 *sigh*) it’s heavy at 157 pounds. It’s also large, at eight feet long and three feet wide, so make sure you have adequate space before splurging. It’s also not the easiest to set up. “Setting this thing up was no joke—I knew I was in for a challenge when I saw the multiple massive, heavy boxes it arrived in,” Appleton says. She notes it took her and a friend two hours to assemble.

Read More: Balanced Body Allegro 2 Review

The classical Merrithew At Home SPX Reformer is next-level if you want to up your Pilates game. It features a foldable vertical tower, which can improve flexibility and target different muscle groups with more controlled movements, adding more challenge. It has five springs—four full-resistance and one with half-resistance. Given the springs mostly have the same resistance, this machine is designed for more advanced users.

The foot bar is adjustable with four positions for different heights, while the carriage is padded for comfort. Another call-out is the included reformer box, which adds height and range of motion to moves in the seated and lying position. It’s especially helpful for those with muscle tightness or who need to modify moves involving the knees.

While this is a great reformer to elevate your practice, it’s quite large at 96 inches long and 26 inches wide. It’s also heavy at 115 pounds. Like the AeroPilates Pro XP 557, this isn’t ideal for apartments. The tower structure also requires more vertical space, so if you don’t have high ceilings, our best overall is most likely your best bet.

Read More: Best Compact Home Gym Equipment

Pretty much all pilates reformers in this guide are relatively large, but the contemporary AeroPilates Reformer 4420 is foldable. If you’re an apartment dweller, this machine is your compact answer to your Pilates reformer dreams. It can be stashed under a couch, bed, or behind a door. At 69 pounds, it’s not the lightest, so having two people for setup is probably your best bet.

Like the AeroPilates Reformer 287, it uses cords, not springs, yet delivers impressive effectiveness. This model has four adjustable cords with varying resistances and color codes, unlike the 287: two standard resistances (black), one extra intensity (red), and one light resistance (yellow). So, this reformer is good for both beginners and those who are more advanced.

It also has a built-in cardio rebounder, which is essentially a mini trampoline at the foot bar, making it an especially good choice for someone looking for low-impact cardio options and variety.

The contemporary Your Reformer is studio-grade like our best overall reformer pick, and is super durable despite being a little over half the price. During a stay in Los Angeles, Appleton rented one for at-home workouts and was extremely impressed with its easily changeable five thick springs, and a carriage that glides smoothly and quietly. The springs are also color-coded: two heavy resistance (red), two medium resistance (blue), and one light resistance (yellow).

In terms of quality, it’s a direct competitor to the Allegro 2. “The straps are thick and definitely won’t fray on me, and the strap handles are comfortable to grip, even when my palms get sweaty,” Appleton says. It’s not compact enough for most apartments, but it’s slimmer to accommodate home spaces better.

Appleton is 5’5” and found the carriage to be wide and spacious, with plenty of room to move around from supine to standing to kneeling positions. It also accommodates her much taller boyfriend, who’s “20 times more passionate about a good reformer workout,” so it’s the real deal.

The AeroPilates Reformer 287 is the most affordable option we’ve come across. It’s dramatically less expensive than our best overall—it costs under $400! But that doesn’t mean it’s less effective. Its quality is still impressive, just not studio-grade. WH entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson, an avid Pilates practitioner, was surprised by how sturdy this machine is because of its bargain price, and since it comes pre-assembled (another plus).

But, she stresses it’s best for beginners since it only features three resistance cords. “I could see someone eventually progressing beyond the capabilities of this model, especially when it comes to exercises like footwork and running, which are classically done on four springs,” says Wilkinson. “It also lacks certain accessories you’d typically find with a studio machine—a box, which is typically used for exercises in the short-box series and in a long position for pulling straps and T-press, among others.”

Speaking of resistance, unlike our best overall, this reformer uses cords instead of springs. While they can be trickier to hook on and off, their weight is identical to springs Wilkinson uses on studio-grade models.The carriage glides smoothly, although Wilkinson notes the attached handles would fall and get in the way. She recommends tossing them aside instead of hanging on the built-in shoulder blocks. As for the foot bar, it’s stable but can’t be adjusted for specific exercises.Aside from mechanics, this reformer is extremely compact, weighing just 56 pounds, and measuring 42 inches when folded and 85 inches fully extended. Wilkinson lives in a one-bedroom Brooklyn apartment and has no issues stashing it away, although she finds it tricky to fold and wide when the foot bar is attached.AeroPilates says this product can fit people up to 6'4", but Wilkinson, who is 5’11”, says even her height was pushing the machine’s limits. “I imagine anyone much taller than I am would feel a bit crunched,” she says. She also says it’s narrow, and didn’t have additional breathing room.

While most full-sized pilates reformers don’t have a built-in trampoline at the foot bar, the contemporary AeroPilates Pro XP 557 is the first full-sized model we’ve seen with a rebounder, so cardio moves like single-leg pushups and slow squats can be added to the routine. This is especially useful for beginners getting into the groove. WH associate visual editor Berkeley Brooks found it stayed sturdy when executing explosive movements at fast paces, while the material of the main carriage prevented her from slipping around.

Brooks notes that the four strong springs are easily interchangeable and have varying resistances labeled by color: two low resistance (blue) and two high resistance (yellow). The foot bar is adjustable, thick, and quiet for added comfort, and can be placed in three positions to accommodate different heights without disrupting your range of motion.

The platform is also wide at 23 inches and long at 100 inches, so this model isn’t ideal for small apartments, especially since you need additional space to execute exercises.

On the upside, Brooks says it’s easy to build and aesthetically pleasing. “I love the addition of wood to the machine because it looks great in a home gym,” she adds.

The springs in a pilates reformer are an important consideration when you’re choosing your machine. “Springs provide resistance and feedback, so the type and responsiveness of springs deeply influence your experience,” says Mo Wolfe, owner and Pilates instructor of Evolution Pilates in Port Washington, New York.

The weight of springs can also depend on whether a machine is classical or contemporary. Classical style reformers have a heavier spring tension that is the same throughout, while modern models generally tend to offer springs with a variety of resistance levels. A reformer with springs is the type you’ll find in a Pilates studio.

Alternatively, resistance cords are sometimes used in the place of springs in reformer machines that are designed for personal and at-home use. They offer similar effectiveness and are more affordable.

Taking the size of your home into consideration is important before purchasing a Pilates machine. Not only do you want to make sure you have enough room for the machine itself, you also want to make sure there will be enough space to perform the full range of Pilates reformer exercises, like leg circles, that require room to move.

Some reformers are very big and bulky, such as our pro-level, best overall selection. They take up considerable real estate and they’re best for a home gym where they can become a more permanent fixture that won’t need to be moved once it’s installed.

If your workout space is multi-functional (i.e., it’s your living room) and your equipment needs to have a smaller footprint and be more portable so you can move it around or stash it away, look for a lighter, foldable option. Just make sure that you’ll have enough space to do the moves when it’s all set up.

Since reformer Pilates is a low-impact activity, and the resistance can be so fine-tuned for your fitness level, there are no hard and fast rules about how often you do a reformer session each week. Miles says it really comes down to how your body feels. “With the variety you can get from a reformer, daily use is manageable. At my studio we have challenging classes, stretch and release classes, technique-focused classes; variety is important!” She notes that most of her clients do three reformer sessions per week.

We picked the brains of Pilates instructors to understand what to look for when shopping for a reformer, then researched dozens of the top-rated models. From there, Women’s Health writers and editors (including fitness contributors Nicolette Accardi and Talene Appleton, and entertainment editor Amy Wilkinson) tested some of the best themselves to narrow down the options.

During testing, they paid close attention to spring and cord resistance level as a measure of whether or not the machines were ideal for beginners or more advanced users. The testers also considered size, durability, and ease of assembly to determine what sorts of spaces were needed for these machiness. Moves like planks, triceps presses, running (pushing off the foot bar), chest expansions, and leg circles were all completed during our testing Pilates workouts to really put these machine to the test.

On November 10, the Wall Street Journal revealed that the model had spent $5.5 million on a home in Crested Butte, about 20 miles south of Aspen. The news came just a day after Hadid hard-launched her new boyfriend, construction project manager Nathan Lacy, whose connection to the area goes back five generations. According to a statement Hadid’s listing agent gave to the WSJ, she had been living in the region for “several months” before pulling the trigger on her unique new digs, built from two coal miner sheds that date to the early 20th century.

Situated just a few feet from Coal Creek, the 2,000-square-foot residence is complete with three bedrooms and three bathrooms. The sellers built the home in 2001, using two existing structures composed of wood and corrugated metal that had stood on the property for 100 years. The sheds were reassembled over a new foundation, with each wooden plank returned to its exact spot on its wall, according to the WSJ. Antique timber from an old Montana mine makes up the rest of the exterior, while pine reclaimed from an 18th-century Virginia barn lines the floors.

A reverse floor plan was designed to let more light into the upper level common areas, like the fireplace-warmed great room, when snow piles up around the ground floor. Reclaimed warehouse beams from a similar time period to the original structures line the vaulted ceiling, with original iron bolts still in place.

#4851. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

You've probably seen this popular laser hair removal device on your social media feeds, and our team says it really does live up to the hype. Nood’s proprietary PrecisionPulse laser makes all of the difference. The IPL flashes every 10 milliseconds, meaning it exposes your skin to less light that could accidentally cause burns.

Nood’s combination of continuous flashes and larger window make it better suited for larger areas, especially the legs. You can polish them off in 15 to 20 minutes, though it's harder to target smaller areas, like the upper lip. We also love the large digital display on this model.

It makes it very easy to toggle through the seven different intensity levels, and it's always clear which one you're working on. The price is friendlier than some other options, plus the brand offers a 90-day money-back guarantee, which makes this device a great option for anyone on the fence about at-home laser hair removal.

There are a lot of laser hair removal devices on the market, which is why you should consider a few of these pointers before investing.

IPL and diode lasers both slow hair growth and reduce the thickness of individual strands by scanning for pigment and targeting the hair follicle, says dermatologist Melanie Kingsley, MD. But, they each have their benefits and limitations.

IPL is the most commonly used type of light in at-home laser hair removal devices. This technology uses broad-spectrum light to target melanin, the pigment that gives your hair its color. The light is also unsuitable for dark and deep skin tones because it can’t distinguish between melanin-rich skin and the pigment of dark hair, says dermatologist Rachel Nazarian, MD. However, if you have a fair to olive complexion with dark hair, then you’re an ideal candidate for IPL treatments.

Until recently, all at-home laser hair removal devices were IPL lasers. But Epilaser has a game-changing laser for home use. Unlike IPL lights, which emit a broad spectrum of light ranging from 400 to 1,400 nm, diode lasers are unique because they use a more concentrated wavelength of light (around 810 nm). This precise wavelength means it can better target the hair follicles rather than accidentally burning your skin, making it more accessible for some people with darker complexions.

Both are effective, but diode lasers are slightly more versatile. That said, no matter which one you go with, you’ll need multiple treatments to maintain your hair-free results.

One of the biggest considerations is the number of flashes a device is equipped to deliver. This number indicates how long the device will last, according to Dr. Nazarian. "Many devices contain about 200,000 flashes, which is typically good for more than 15 years, although it also depends on how many areas you’re treating," she says. Other recommendations on this list, like the Smoothskin, have unlimited flashes, which means they'll theoretically last forever, but are pricier.

Extra features like multiple intensity modes—lower options for sensitive skin; higher settings for those who want to see results fast (see the Nood)—or interchangeable heads for precise treatment all over the body (hi, Braun) can increase the price. The amount you spend comes down to the features you want in your device and how long you want it to last.

One of the best ways to reduce discomfort during laser hair removal is to use cooling technology. It lowers your skin’s temperature—before, during, and after each laser pulse—to help you better tolerate longer and higher treatment settings safely.

Devices with bigger heads are more efficient on large areas. For more targeted flashes, opt for rigs with compact heads, such as the Iouniya Laser Hair Removal, which can be used on both the face and body. If you have sensitive skin, consider stretching your treatments out to once a month to start and gradually up the frequency once your skin can handle the laser hair removal treatment. The final hair-free results will take longer to achieve but at least you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, she says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

Once you choose your device, know that it can take some time to see results. While every device is different, you’ll probably use it weekly anywhere from four to 10 weeks before noticing lasting results, says dermatologist Bertha Baum, DO. The final results might take longer to achieve, but you won’t risk irritating your skin. FWIW, warm weather likely won’t return until April or early May, meaning you’ve got several weeks to achieve smooth results. Either way, Dr. Baum says you’ll notice thinning hair after your first four treatments.

This technology has come a long way and, while pricey, it's a long-term investment that pays for itself. Think of it this way: A laser that costs $500 is basically the same price as a professional hair removal session, and that in-office treatment won't last forever, but you will continue using your at-home laser for years. And FWIW, we found a few discounted, top-rated Amazon picks that start at just $42, but you’ll want to hurry since these are fleeting deals.

At Women’s Health, we prioritize hands-on editor testing to ensure you don’t waste your time or money. Ahead is insight on what went into our editorial process while trying the latest and greatest at-home laser hair removal devices.

After testing these devices since February 2022, beauty director Brian Underwood, deputy deals and trends editor Eunice Lucero-Lee, and luxury commerce editor Sarah Maberry whittled down this list to 12 of the best laser hair removal devices. We also tapped contributors Jasmine Gomez, Lily Wohlner, and Brigitt Earley to ensure these devices work across most skin tones.

They all boast impressive features, are comfortable to use, and offer incredible value. Plus, these picks are FDA-cleared, so they’ve been evaluated for safety and efficacy. Several dermatologists also shared their no-fail laser hair removal tips and best-in-class product recommendations.

And because we know what it’s like to ball on a budget, we also considered pricing. TBH, laser hair removal devices aren’t exactly cheap. Many cost between $300 and $600, especially when shopping for these expert-approved devices from well-respected brands, such as Braun.

To help, I carefully researched dozens of other cheaper, yet top-rated Amazon laser hair removal devices. Ultimately, I found four Amazon picks that are aligned with expert guidance and are currently discounted as low as $35. Talk about major savings! For added peace of mind, they all earned thousands of rave reviews from real Amazon customers.

So if you're ready to ditch daily shaving and bi-monthly waxing, we're confident—based on our own testing and our dermatologists' advice—that this list contains only the best, most effective options on the market worth your hard-earned coins.

Dr. Nazarian confirms at-home laser hair removal devices are generally safe and effective, citing a 2019 paper. The biggest challenge with many at-home devices comes down to their inability to differentiate between dark skin and dark hair due to their pigmentation. Melanin-rich complexions risk absorbing too much laser energy that increases the risk for burning, cautions Dr. Nazarian. If this is you, then see your dermatologist for a recommendation on the best laser hair removal treatments and devices.

It's also a good idea to do a patch test and not expose the treated area to sunlight for a week, says Dr. Shirazi. Your treated skin is temporarily more sensitive, and you risk sunburn, hyperpigmentation, and delayed healing. She also doesn’t suggest using the laser on tanned and tattooed skin, open wounds, moles, or birthmarks to avoid changing their appearance or causing accidental burns.

Truthfully, they're not optimal for sensitive or dark skin. Many at-home devices cannot distinguish between melanin-rich complexions and dark hair, says dermatologist Corey L. Hartman, MD. Anyone else can still give them a try.

And, like with salon treatments, it's important to practice patience—this isn't a "one and done" situation. Many devices need to be used multiple times weekly to achieve the initial results. Plus, each at-home session can take 10 to 60 minutes, depending on how much body and facial hair you plan to remove. While a tad annoying upfront, this minor inconvenience has a major payoff because your hair will regrow slower over time with regular use.

#4847. ‘The Gilded Age’ Star Ben Ahlers and Todd Snyder Know the Power of a Good Uniform

For the label’s latest campaign, the 30-year-old actor takes fall style to Scotland’s Isle of Islay.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

TODD SNYDER makes some of our favorite menswear, and for its latest collaboration, the New York brand crossed the pond to Scotland. The draw? Lagavulin, the distillery that’s been making smoky Scotch whisky on the island of Islay for more than 200 years.

The partnership marks Snyder’s 15th anniversary, with clothes that borrow from Islay’s rugged landscape. Standouts include a brown suede jacket lined in Lagavulin’s own tartan and Fair Isle zip-ups in the earthy shades of the Scottish moors. Pretty great reasons to look forward to sweater weather.

Fronting the campaign is Ben Ahlers. As footman-turned-businessman Jack Trotter on The Gilded Age, the 30-year-old actor knows his way around heritage menswear. Still, these relaxed layers are pretty easy to picture on the streets of New York. We caught up with him about what playing Jack taught him about getting dressed—and which piece he’d bring home.

MEN’S HEALTH: You spend a lot of time in period costumes on The Gilded Age. Has anything from Jack’s wardrobe made its way into how you dress off-screen?

BEN AHLERS: Jack has a consistency to the way that he dresses. As a footman, he had a uniform, and as a young businessman, he has a pretty steady throughline through his looks—a base structure with really well-made clothing and then accents like a tie or a tie pin or a ring that can allow for a sense of creative expression. I find that I like a level of consistency in my own personal dress as well.

More than anything, the greatest benefit of living inside of the clothing that Kasia [Walicka Maimone, the show’s costume designer] and her incredible team make for us every year is this awareness of the way clothes not only make you present to the world but also how they make you feel within them.

MH: Is there a menswear trend from that era you wish more guys would embrace today?

BA: I would love to see some of the creativity come out in menswear and in the accent work, like a tie pin. Some of the tie pins we have on this show are just so well-crafted and specific. The heads of canes the men wore back then also have such an artistry to them, and there aren’t a lot of avenues for that sort of expression in modern menswear. It’d be nice to see that creative voice or risk-taking come through in the subtle accents that we wear in our day-to-day life.

MH: Your role in Death of a Salesman got people talking about your physique. How did you prepare?

BA: For Death of a Salesman, I knew earlier on in the development process that they wanted to go the direction that they did for the top of the show, and so I knew that I was going to be kind of exposed every night. I really tried to go to the gym during the rehearsal process because I knew once we opened the show that it was going to be hard to stay as active—the show was just so draining.

The couple of months up to opening, I really made a practice of five days a week of cross-training, lifting, running, and yoga, and trying to keep my body as nimble and buoyant as possible, because the subject matter and the daily grind of showing up to the theater every day can really take a toll.

During the run, a lot of my focus was on rest, recovery, sauna, cold plunge, diet, stretching, because I’d already built the foundation of the physicality. Throughout the five-month run, it came down to being sure that I was healthy and recovering as best as I could.

MH: What happened between takes on the Todd Snyder shoot that we’d never know from looking at the campaign photos?

BA: Between takes, I had a blast with Boo George, our photographer. He is such a character and one of the best energies on set, and really delivered in the work. The whole crew from Todd Snyder and Lagavulin were so supportive, and it was such a fun little escape for all of us to exist on this island in the most beautiful landscape imaginable.

I really enjoyed getting to know a lot of the locals there. Many of the people there worked at the distillery, and I got to see firsthand how the whisky was actually made. People were so proud to share their culture as well as their craft with the world.

MH: Which piece from the collection would you wear back home in New York, and what would you pair it with?

BA: My favorite piece from the collection is the Todd Snyder x Lagavulin suede stable jacket, inspired by the texture and color of the mossy peat that coats Islay. It’s a perfect fall jacket, and I’d pair it with Todd Snyder’s relaxed barrel jean in khaki, which I think would really pop.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4846. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

Some additional features: The hood is just the right size—big enough to keep Nied’s head warm without causing a hair disaster. It has multiple closures, like buttons and zippers down the front. Nied is usually a size medium, and says this coat runs true-to-size. The sleeves come with a snug, sweater-like fabric at the end that she can pull over her hands to keep them warm, and the sleeves are also long enough to cover her arms comfortably.

As for warmth, this coat delivers. It’s super warm without even zipping it up—even in near-freezing temps and wind. Nied says it’s definitely the coat she'll wear when the temps plunge to zero for holiday festivities. That’s because the outside is made from a blend of cotton and polyester, which is durable and water-repellent. It’s also made with a 625 fill power made from responsibly sourced down, meaning this jacket keeps you comfortable in temps ranging from fourteen to negative four degrees Fahrenheit. The length, which hits at mid-thigh, also helps keep the chill out.

The only con we have for this jacket is the main pockets. They are lined with fleece that is so cozy for hands, but they have button-up closures instead of zippers, so our things don’t feel as secure.

WH lifestyle director Lindsay Geller is a dog owner, which means she's out early in the morning and late at night to get her pup some exercise. But, since the weather has dropped, she's been on the hunt for a coat she can wear at the chilliest times of the day to keep her warm all walk long. Lucky for her, she got to test this puffer from lululemon, which she says she's "obsessed" with.

This jacket is super sleek and basically covers your entire outfit with its calf-length design, so it's easy to throw it on over any outfit and call it a day. "I wouldn't wear this coat to a formal winter event like a wedding party, but I would pretty much wear it everywhere else like running errands or on a cold vacation," says Geller. "I wish I'd had this coat when I went to Norway last year—it would have been perfect for that."

Geller chose the black color, which she's happy about as it's super easy to style, and goes with pretty much everything.

Because this is one of lululemon's warmest jackets, you would think it would be too hot and bulky to run in, but Geller says that she was surprised at how easily it moved with her body during a morning run with her pup. "I'm used to long puffers feeling super bulky, but this one doesn't," she says, adding that it's still snug and insulated enough to keep her warm. Geller opted for a size medium, and she notes that it fits "just right." She told me that she's worn this coat on freezing cold winter mornings, and it feels like she's wrapped in an "insanely warm, yet still remarkably lightweight blanket" the entire time. "Safe to say, I'll be living in this coat until spring (at least)," she says.

Her main con is the zipper can be tricky to maneuver at the bottom, but once you hear it click, it works. However, she says it can get frustrating just trying to get the bottom part of the zipper to work.

"I absolutely adore my Columbia down jacket," says WH news and features editor Currie Engel. It's her go-to jacket for all her winter occasions.

"Lately, I've been rocking it everywhere—from the gym to dates and even at work," she says. That’s because it strikes a perfect style balance, with no over-the-top designs that lean too casual or too fancy—except maybe the fur-lined hood (which is removable!). And with a relaxed silhouette, it flatters the body without looking too bulky—despite the slightly longer mid-thigh length. This makes it a match for anything in her wardrobe.Engel opted for a size medium, and she notes that it fits perfectly. "I was able to fit my wallet, phone, keys, and more in there with absolute ease (and no bulges!)." She adds that the outer fabric, which is made of polyester, is *super* luxurious and thick without the hefty price tag. The insulated interior is made of the brand's patented Omni-Heat Reflective lining, which reflects and retains body heat without adding bulk. Plus, the outer is made with 100 percent polyester, which is a welcome bonus because its small synthetic fibers help keep you super warm, and is water-resistant to help wick away sweat or light rain. It’s also insulated with 100% synthetic down—making it a more affordable option that still keeps you warm in cold, rainy weather.While there weren't many cons, Engel told me she wishes the hood could zip off.

This puffer goes all the way down past the knee to keep you nice and protected (and extra warm!). TBH, it’s hard to find a long puffer that’s actually flattering. This jacket looks just as great with a pair of slim-fit jeans and loafers as it does with ski pants and boots.

One thing we ran into a lot with long coats is that they were too long for more petite people, but we found that this one hits at the calf no matter what height you are, short or tall. We do find that, in terms of puffers, we like the soft, airy texture of the Super Puff better than this option, as it’s a bit on the heavier side.

While the SuperPuff is on the pricier side, it’s well worth the investment for its durability and performance in harsh weather, says Saladino. “It’s not just a winter coat—it’s a statement piece that’s both functional and fashionable,” she says. Case in point: It comes in a variety of colors and lengths depending on your preference. Even the shorter hip-length version Saladino tested came in clutch for staying warm while on the go.

It stands out as one of the most stylish winter coats with its luxe, oversized fit and wide stitched panels that give it an edgy look. We also love the matte, nylon outer material and monochrome buttons that look super clean. It’s effortlessly chic and doesn’t skimp on function.

Warmth will not be questioned in this puffer. Saladino wore this during a brutally cold NYC afternoon and found that it kept her incredibly cozy. How? It’s filled with 700-plus fill-power premium down that provides some major insulation. The nylon outer is also water-repellent and wind-resistant, so you don’t have to panic if you get stuck in harsh conditions.

We appreciate that this coat has zippered pockets, so our belongings never fall out. Another bonus feature: It comes with a detachable hood. And we were pleasantly surprised that this coat runs true-to-size. We opted for our normal size and found that there was still room to fit a hoodie underneath.

This jacket is extremely warm with its fleece interior and 100% synthetic insulation, but it’s also one of the most durable options on this list. Its silicone-coated nylon exterior is water-repellent, so it keeps you dry if you get stuck in the rain or snow. Plus, it’s made with a wind-fighting nylon tech for extreme weather conditions, making it great for winter hikers. Although it has all these features, we found that the coat actually still feels lightweight. A bonus point is that it’s shorter than many other coats on this list, so it’s not as bulky and doesn't feel restrictive.

We also love that it comes with a hood, but it’s not removable, which marked it down a few points in our book. That being said, this coat is great for harsher conditions. Another pro? This coat comes equipped with plenty of pockets, including interior ones. So, when you’re out and about, you don’t have to worry about where you’re going to store your belongings.

In terms of size, we def recommend sizing down because this coat can look super bulky if it’s too big. However, we found that sizing down eliminated some of the thickness in the coat.

Many jackets on this list are water-resistant, but this option from Rains is fully waterproof. It kept our tester dry in light rain, thanks to the water-repellent finish. On top of that, we found this jacket to be breathable, lightweight, and super-durable. Even in the harsh NYC winds, we found that it protected us from the elements and kept us warm and dry.

Style contributor Rose Lauture recently went on a trip to Vermont and tested this coat while she was out there. “As soon as I walked out from the airport and felt the chilly air hit my face, I knew I made the right decision wearing this coat,” she says. We also appreciate that it comes in a variety of matte and shiny colors, so there are plenty of options to choose from. However, you can easily throw it in the washer with cold water to clean it.

As far as fit goes, it is a bit oversized, but since it’s supposed to have more of that streetstyle look, we like its slightly larger fit. Want it to be a bit more snug? Opt for one size down.

In our opinion, a puffer jacket is a must-have for every wardrobe because it keeps you warm and pairs great with any outfit. But through our testing, we’ve learned that not all puffers are created equally—until we discovered this one from The North Face.

Despite its shorter length, it’s one of the best options on our list for braving the cold, thanks to ultra-warm 700-fill down insulation and an insulated hood that seamlessly packs into the collar. It’s also made with a durable nylon outer and lining, making this a great water-resistant and moisture-wicking option, too.

“This jacket is one of the warmest offerings from The North Face, and it’s also windproof, making it perfect for braving those chilly winter days,” says Saladino. Her fave feature? The tuckable hood. She loves how easy it is to fold into the collar when it’s not in use.

We also love the retro vibe of this winter jacket. It has a boxy, relaxed fit that’s super chic and flattering. According to Saladino, it has a timeless look that feels both classic and fresh. “The zip pockets on the outside are super practical, and the interior pocket means I can leave my handbag behind during the colder months,” says Saladino. “Overall, it’s a stylish, functional, and incredibly cozy choice for cold weather.” The entire jacket also easily stows into the right-hand pocket, so it’s super easy to pack.

Our one recommendation? Size up for a roomier fit. We found that going true-to-size left us feeling a bit too snug and unable to layer heavier clothing underneath. REI doesn't currently carry this red shade, but it has a cute berry colorway and neutral options to choose from.

Before buying a winter coat, think about where you’ll be using it. Are you living in a big city or a rural area? Does it get crazy cold or more temperate in the winter? How active are you? Once you've decided what you need, you can get into the nitty-gritty of coat shopping.

The key to a warm winter coat? Insulation. But there are two main types to consider: down and synthetic. Learning a bit about them can guide you in choosing the right coat for your lifestyle.

The bottom line: If you live in a wet environment and want to spend less money, go with synthetic insulation. If you live in a drier, colder place and are willing to splurge a bit more, opt for a coat that has down insulation.

You want to make sure your winter jacket is warm enough to last through many seasons. And, in order to do that, you want to make sure the materials your jacket is made of are super weather-resistant, especially if you’re in an area with harsh conditions and need extra warmth and protection. #4840. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4839. How to Self-Actualise

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Self-actualisation is one of the oldest themes of therapy. It is present in all the founders, especially Jung’s notion of individuation, Carl Rogers’ sublime book On Becoming a Person, and Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, with self-actualisation on top. Yet few have ever outlined how to do self-actualisation in any systematic way.

I have a go at it in my book Beyond Happy, drawing on perspectives from humanistic psychology, existentialist philosophy, and more recent ideas in quantitative psychological science. I’ll sketch my approach here.

A useful place to start is self-discrepancy theory. It argues that we have a sense of three self concepts:

Begin by developing a thorough understanding of how each of these manifests in you. A journal can help.

Be mindful of what in your ideal and ought self is authentic to you versus a product of your environment or socialisation. The influence of family and trusted peers can be benevolent and beneficial, but you first need to get some distance from it if you want self-discovery.

The next step is self-creation: Bring your actual self into alignment with your ideal self, subject to the constraint imposed by your ought self.

This might require some tricky harmonisation. Consider a young woman who aspires to be a judge on the International Court of Justice. There’s a fast track there through commercial law, but she feels queasy about representing immoral companies. This is her ought self speaking, and harmonisation might require taking a slower route, perhaps through environmental law instead.

Your ideal self doesn’t need to be ambitious; indeed, that might be wholly unsuitable for you. Your ideal self is simply the person you’d be most proud to be. You might want to be a folksy type with lots of spare time to help friends and enjoy an array of hobbies. Stay true to yourself.

Now your first guess at your ideal self is likely to be wrong. Self-actualisation is an iterative process, and you’ll learn by doing.

That learning comes principally in the form of affective feedback. Joy, serenity, exhilaration and other positive emotions are signals to invest more.

What about negative feedback? Self-discrepancy theory finds that depression attends discrepancies between the actual and ideal self, while anxiety is associated with actual-ought self discrepancies. But you need to introspect to understand what these feelings mean for you in each case.

Are you depressed because your ideal self is meaningful to you and you’re not living up to it? Then that negative emotion is a signal to try harder.

But if you’re depressed because achieving your ideal is hard and feels like a drag, that’s a two-part affective signal. There’s depression, but also a lack of enthusiasm.

Here we get our next big self-actualisation puzzle piece from self-determination theory: There are five varieties of motivation running on a spectrum from extrinsic to relatively intrinsic.

Extrinsically motivated activities are done under duress. They require a great deal of self-regulation to enact because you don’t want to do them.

Introjected activities are done for a reason contingent to the activity itself. For example, many people put up with exercise because they want to be healthy.

We’re more autonomous here, but there’s still a lot of self-regulation going on, so these activities tend to drain our willpower and feel exhausting. If there’s no sense of achievement afterwards, then the activity is likely unsustainable.

The depressed and demotivated individual above is probably doing something introjected. The lack of enthusiasm is a signal that it’s not authentic to them.

They should switch to something with intrinsic motivation. These activities are self-determined, which means we do them spontaneously for their own sake. They’re associated with feelings of interest and vitality.

Not everything in the ideal and ought selves will be intrinsically motivated. Indeed, when self-actualisation begins, it usually involves a lot of identified motivation. This is where we value something but don’t have intrinsic motivation for it.

I value being honest, for example, but it didn’t come naturally to me. Indeed, it took at least a decade of deliberate effort to stop telling white lies.

Introjected and identified motivations can be internalised over time until they become intrinsic, but sustaining the necessary effort requires payoffs in the form of frequent positive feedback.

For example, I loathed mathematics in school. But training in it has made me a better social scientist, for which I have intrinsic motivation. Seeing the ways math would help me achieve this part of my ideal self kept me going through my statistics classes. Nowadays maths comes much more easily to me; it’s not a joy, but I don’t notice it enough to loathe it anymore.

This is an example of integrated motivation – where something identified becomes connected to something intrinsically motivated, and so is easier to engage in.

Let me bring this all together in a simple model of self-actualisation, shown in the image below. Imagine a young woman who dreams of being an astronaut. She identifies two activities as central to this ideal self – science and athletics, so she enrols in chemistry and a gymnastics club.

As she goes about these activities, she gets feedback. Maybe she likes gymnastics, but this particular club is full of overly competitive people. Introspecting on this feedback, she realises that gymnastics is right for her; she just needs to join a more casual club.

She loves chemistry, but her casual interest in gymnastics means she won’t be fit enough to be an astronaut. She needs to recalibrate her ideal self. Maybe she can be a terrestrial scientist and study samples sent by the astronauts to her lab.

This cycle of goal, feedback, introspection, and recalibration takes place across all facets of your life, slowly bringing them into harmony and yourself into actualisation.

Ryan, R., & Deci, E. (2017). Self-Determination Theory: Basic Psychological Needs in Motivation, Development, and Wellness. Guildford.

Higgins, E. T. (1987). Self-discrepancy: A theory relating self and affect. Psychological Review, 94(3), 319–340.
