#4816. This Is Still the Best Water Bottle I've Ever Used

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

YOUR WATER BOTTLE is an expression of yourself. Sure, you're buying the thing for its functionality and design, but you’re also buying into what the water bottle represents. Whether you’re in need of an all-metal wide mouth for outdoor trekking, an insulated squeeze bottle for home gym power hours, or a smart water bottle that can track your daily intake, we've got the best water bottle to fit your hydration needs below.

Most importantly, you're buying a water bottle to nourish your body and give it the liquid it requires. Now, precise water intake depends on the person and how active they are. We do know that it's not always easy to throw back the H2O, but the benefits are many and there are easy tricks to drinking more water, which will only benefit the body. Having a high-functioning, reusable water bottle you enjoy using will keep you high-functioning as well.

As a study last year found, most adults are not getting enough in terms of daily water intake. That may seem trivial, and perhaps even equate to fewer trips to the bathroom, but there are real health concerns there. Proper hydration can reduce the risk of disease and injury, aid with recovery, and much more. So, let us embrace making it as easy as possible to get the right amount of water we all need.

The Yeti Yonder water bottle has been a go-to for several of our editors for a few years now. The chug spout and cap design is perfect for everyday use, not too narrow or wide. The BPA-free plastic construction is so tough that it's been through drops onto concrete from 10 feet high (it accidentally fell off the top of an SUV when one editor was visiting family in Kansas City). Another big reason why we chose a plastic water bottle as our best overall pick is due to weight—the Yonder is much lighter than its metal counterparts. Unless you're doing some serious hiking or camping, the Yonder will essentially serve multiple uses without any questioning of keeping liquid cold or durability.

The Yonder hardly ever leaks either, no matter which cap you choose. We personally like the add-on Yonder Tether Cap. It makes the bottle a little more streamlined and takes off even more weight. But, the traditional cap it comes with is solid too and might actually be easier to carry by itself. And we've found the 25 oz size to be the sweet spot.

Last detail to point out is price and number of colors available. Sometimes Yeti gear can get expensive. This is not the case with the Yonder water bottles. Pick and choose from all the new colors the brand releases over time. Build a small collection. Gift a few. This is our favorite water bottle we've used over the years.

This is a more practical version for on-the-go guys who want to see what the Stanley craze is about. The slim design makes it slide into backpacks and gym bags with ease, and its pop-top cap is simple and secure. The cap design actually uses a two-step locking process to help avoid accidentally opening (which is a huge plus for those of us who've used these types of water bottles in the past). But it's not like cracking a safe, as the thing opens with relative ease for that quick pull of water when you need it right away.

The Quick Flip Go's double-wall-insulated design means it can keep cold drinks cold and hot drinks hot. One of our editors has even used it to sip morning coffee from time to time. We imagine it would even keep some white wine chilled in a backyard setting, too.

So why is this water bottle not our top pick? It comes down to weight. The Quick Flip Go is just a tad heavier than the Yeti Yonder. If you can get over the weight detail, though, then this pick is just as valid as a top choice.

Can a water bottle be playful? The radiant color scheme here suggests so. And why not, this is the tool that should accompany you on a lot of joyous outings, from cycling through country roads to hiking in the woods. Choose from a host of three sizes (24 oz is our preferred capacity) and enjoy the FreeSip Spout, which pivots to and from big gulps and sipping from a straw seamlessly.

The carry loop is ergonomic and folds into the bottle and push-button access means no leaks. While relatively slender overall, we found that the bottle had no problem taking on scoops of ice with the lid fully off. And once that ice is in place, you're set for 24 hours of polar temperatures. About the only scenario in which this bottle struggles is for athletes competing in helmet sports, as the broad mouth can't get through a lot of face guards. But you could also just take that helmet off before hydrating.

With so many rave reviews in favor of this bottle, it was a little hard to approach it as a skeptic. But that's what good testers do, and we came in thinking there was no way it could match the hype. Almost immediately in our testing we were proved wrong. This is a contemporary water bottle for the contemporary world and once you have one, you never want to go back to the old way.

Why does it slap? Aesthetic, durability, and a high-functioning nature. The handle is one of the best we've used, the build is sturdy, and the associated app is all kinds of helpful. It self-cleans in a single minute, insulates for a full day, and there's even a hydration tracker to keep you swigging when you should be.

The handle is detachable and the bottle itself filters the contents, making for a clean sip every time. The look is among the best out there and the color options are great too. Complaints? Few and far between, although the drinking sensors can be a little buggy and the nozzle is tricky to clean. But overall, it's a gem.

Basic squeeze water bottles for the gym are okay for use, but if you're looking for a much more enjoyable way to stay hydrated while working out then you'll want to try the Camelbak Podium. This water bottle is under $20 (sometimes even lower depending on the sale) and comes with an insulated design that keeps cold water from covering the outside of it—which means no condensation will be soaking your hands in between sets.

The spout and cap design is another huge sell for why we love the Podium for the gym. The top is designed to keep away dirt for mountain bikers, but when transferred to the gym it means there's no leakage when falling over and no gross gym dust and germs floating where you put your mouth. The spout is also similar to drinking out of a Camelbak backpack, which a few of our editors found novel.

The Podium is a little outside the box for what you'd think of as a gym water bottle, but its insulation and high level of leak-proofing makes it seriously good for all types of active settings. It doesn't hurt that it has a cool design, too.

Familiar, durable, and affordable is what makes Nalgene so good after so many years. The brand offers a ton of fun colors, designs, and patterns, so you have a full array of ways to express yourself. However, we realize the design of your Nalgene might not matter as much if you plan on layering it with all the cool stickers you collect on your travels.

Does it have insulation or specialized cap designs for sipping? No, but that's not the point. Nalgene water bottles are all about keeping things minimalist. Over time, it might start to leak a little bit or get beaten up by the dishwasher. If that happens, find a way to recycle and buy a new one for less than $20. Overall, this is a modern classic of a water bottle that's about as durable as they come. We've even run them over with mountain bikes and small cars and didn't even put a dent in 'em. The simplicity means it's also noticeably easier to clean.

Toughness with a simple design that appeals to the bare-bones hydrators out there. We like to think they’re just old enough now they’ve become somewhat iconic, earning a following for all camps, from classroom commuters to weekend warrior backcountry hikers.

If there was a water bottle we might want to bring to a deserted island, this might be it. That's because it excels in versatility, able to do just about whatever you need it to do. We appreciated the wide mouth, which delivered big swigs after long jogs or paddles on a SUP. There was never any spilling thanks to a leakproof spout and the hinge lock is a nice accent, especially if you're on the active side and like to have your water bottle with you on those adventures.

The extra large clip is nice for outings like hikes and travel and we found the insulation to be pretty good, keeping things chilled for at least 12 hours even in warm conditions. It's easy to clean, whether by hand or in the machine, and it fits in every cup holder we tried, from cars to strollers. If you need an extra nudge of insulation, just pack the thing with ice. We found the bottle to be a bit weaker than others in terms of durability (can dent up if you're hard on the thing) but for the price, it's a nice option indeed.

You really can't go wrong with any Hydro Flask, but this 32-ounce water bottle came to be our favorite from our editors who like to hike and camp, and from those who enjoy a high-capacity water bottle. The wide mouth design at the top makes for fast drinking as well as easy pouring and cleaning. As for the material, you've got insanely durable stainless steel with double wall insulation at your service.

This water bottle fits well in most hiking backpacks and duffel bags, despite its larger size. We liked how secure the cap and handle are too, as it allows for one-handed carry when walking short distances.

You're buying excellence with this water bottle. It's going to stay strong for years, no matter what adventures you throw at it. Outdoorsy types especially should consider this model if they're in need of a water bottle.

We liked the first edition of the Hidrate Spark PRO and the second round only improves on the original. It’s an entire hydration program tied to an ultra contemporary bottle and helpful sibling app. You can customize your intake based on your activities and track your progress right down to the drop.

The bottle itself is sweatproof. We appreciated the fact that it rarely if ever slipped out of our paws, even amid a grueling workout. The double-insulation does its job and the recycled 18/8 stainless steel is a nice touch. Also, the lid performed well, even outdoors, with a protective lid, a large carrying handle, and a chug spout for when you’re really thirsty.

When you get a higher IQ bottle such as this, it can sometimes be a little demanding, Not the case here. The newest option from Hidrate does insist that you stay hydrated, but in subtle fashion, with the occasional glow or beep. It’s much better than a bottle that nudges too hard, causing the user to revolt and ignore the thing.

Smart as this water bottle is, it still requires some babying when it comes to washing. The sensor is especially sensitive and should be cleaned with care. But that’s a small price to pay for a water bottle that essentially serves as your personal hydration coach.

There are a handful of filtered water bottles on the market, but no brand has wowed us more than LifeStraw. For starters, the LifeStraw filter is one of the most trusted designs on the market. According to the brand, the two-stage filtration will eliminate 99.999999% of bacteria (including E. coli and Salmonella), and 99.999% of microplastics, sand, and dirt. LifeStraw then packed its filter inside the stainless steel bottle, which we found to be much more appealing than plastic models where you can see the filter inside.

The cost of the Lifestraw Go here is a little elevated, but you are paying for the special filter. You do need to change the LifeStraw filter inside about every 60 days, so that's an extra cost. The payoff though, from what our editors discovered, is the peace of mind you get filling up your water bottle at a public water fountain or from tap water that comes out of a sink.

Grab this water bottle if you're looking for a filtered option with excellent design. There are times when you can’t fully trust your water source but this vessel affords peace of mind (and no bickering of the gut).

To say these bottles were tested is an understatement. Over the course of several years, various Men's Health editors and I put them to work—like, overtime. We paired them up with the most active members of our team, allowing us to get a clean picture of just how well these bottles perform. Hot weather, cold weather, in the gym, out on the trail, on the saddle of a bike, on plane rides, or just commuting; we brought them everywhere.

Throughout the process, we paid close attention to various attributes. Obviously, we wanted a water bottle that looks good. But more importantly, we wanted a water bottle that made staying hydrated easy, thoughtless, and perhaps even enjoyable. We analyzed design, material, size, and special features. We waded through reputable reviews and talked up insiders in the outdoors recreation and sporting worlds for their takes. And of course, we looked at price.

In the end, the Yeti has won us over on all fronts. Durable, lightweight, packable, and super affordable, it has been a favorite among many testers since it released in 2022. But several others came close, offering different traits like filtration, improved insulation, or more sophisticated lids.

Some people prefer wide-mouth tops on their water bottles for faster drinking, while others prefer a spout design that's much smaller and easier to sip. Really it comes down to preference, but there are spout designs we tested that are more enjoyable to drink from than others. Do keep in mind that lots of companies make tops that are interchangeable in case you want to switch to a different design.

To avoid any contamination of plastics, most water bottles we reviewed came in a metal design. There are some plastic water bottles we tested, however, that were BPA-free and we found to not have any impact on taste. Our top-tested water bottle from Yeti is actually made from BPA-free plastic. Our editors have tested this water bottle for nearly two years and have found no issues with taste or with material breakdown from a dishwasher.

Material also dictates temperature retention, with things like double-insulated stainless steel keeping things nice and chilled for long periods of time. Plastic tends to not insulate quite as well, but can be quite durable (and recycled). Keep this in mind as you weigh how important an ice-cold pull of water is to you.

How much water are you going to need? Capacity is a vital consideration, as you might just be looking for a little hydration while at work (where you can continue to refill when necessary) or be out and about all weekend at the campground, potentially away from a water source. Less volume is just fine for quicker outings or when you want to be streamlined, like on a bike. But you'll be wanting additional capacity for, say, lengthy conferences, road trips, or exhausting workout routines.

There are a few water bottles we selected thanks to special features our editors love. Lifestraw, for example, provides some of the best water filtration you can buy. The fact Lifestraw discreetly hides its filter behind a stainless steel body is a huge reason why we featured it on our list. The same goes for the Camelbak Podium, as its insulated body and cap and spout design make it especially suitable for indoor gym settings.

Yes. A reusable bottle is easier on the planet for that very reason—it's reusable. Single-use plastic is wasteful stuff and, worse, it does not decompose, likely ending up in the ocean and your food supply chain (not to mention turning into microplastic). Going with a bottle like the ones listed here does require some energy and inputs upfront, but because it's your long-term bottle (don't go losing it now), the carbon footprint is less.

You can take it a step further by purchasing a bottle made with responsibly sourced materials, sometimes even made from up-cycled or recycled materials. Look for non-BPA (a bad chemical) options and preferably ones that use very little if no plastic. Glass and stainless steel are generally easier on Mother Earth. And be good to yourself by keeping the thing clean and sterile.

Here's the thing about mold: It likes wet environments. You know, like inside of your water bottle. It's a repulsive thought, but some of that gunk buildup in your vessel might just be mold. Don't fret, you can clean the thing.

Now, it would take a fair amount of mold to sicken the average person but regardless, a clean water bottle is just worth having. Wash your bottle daily, either in the dishwasher if it's permitted or by hand, ideally with hot water and a scrub to get into those nooks and crannies—water bottle brushes are a great tool.

Occasionally, consider a more intense clean. Do to the bottle as you might to your coffee maker, soaking it in a mix of vinegar and water. Even the occasional boiling water soak will help keep the bottle pristine.

#4814. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

AS WE START to inch closer and closer to the end of the year, we know you’re going to be looking to feel cozy as the weather starts to get colder. Luckily, there are plenty of exciting sci-fi and fantasy books to curl up with a big mug of something hot with and read next to a fire.

There's new releases from mainstays like Jim Butcher and Matt Dinniman (two in fact, plus an upcoming TV show). There's all manner of space operas, cyberpunk thrillers, quests to kill gods, and even a wolf who sets out to kill the human race. And toward the end of the year, Emily St. John Mandel of Station Eleven fame returns with a new hopeful futuristic tale. As summer winds down, new books will continue to offer a much-needed escape throughout 2026.

Admittedly, there's been a lot of media begging for our attention this year, like The Odyssey, the World Cup, and soon Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three. But once the adrenaline of those action-packed watches wear off, it'll be the perfect time to crack open a new read and lock into assassins dealing with an alien invasion or a botched quest to clone the founding fathers (seriously).

Below is our list of the best reads of the year no matter what kind of sci-fi or fantasy you're interested in. Keep checking back as the year continues to progress for more updates.

A group of civilians are chosen to accompany veteran astronauts on a trip to Saturn's moon, Titan. They struggle to orbit the planet, and after some struggle, they manage to get back on course and return to Earth. But the Earth they left doesn't seem to be the planet they remember.

The 18th (yes, 18th!) book in Butcher's long-running Dresden Files series finds its titular character, Harry Dresden, struggling with grief. But Chicago is struggling, his brother is seriously ill, and he's now betrothed to a vampire. He'll have to put his own feelings aside to be the wizard everyone needs him to be.

Think dating is hard right now? Maybe you'll find solace in For Human Use, where a new app helps people find love with cadavers. You read that right. And as the app gains popularity, two men behind its funding and growth are pitted against one another.

Best known for his Dungeon Crawler Carl series, Matt Dinniman is back with a standalone novel. Oliver lives on the planet New Sonora, but when Earth decides to evict the planet's tenants, they make a deadly game of it, allowing Earth's gamers to use war machines for fun. Oliver decides to try and save his home no matter what.

Leena can see the dead, but keeps her secret closely guarded. When her brother falls ill, she decides to bargain away her secret to a dangerous merchant. Her trade leads her to a mysterious estate, where she has to fight for her life to escape the merchant's grasp.

The first in a new trilogy, Tao Wong's The First Step follows a young farmer who joins a school of cultivation, and begins a magical journey filled with martial arts, Chinese mythology, and a chance at immortality.

It's post-WWI Britain, and what people hope to be a time of peace is overtaken by a new threat. Fae are taking children, and one vet decides he'll be the one to bring them back.

If you don't normally read short story collections, now's your chance. Featuring award-winning and nominated stories, this book may be the perfect read to get you out of a reading slump with tales you can finish in one sitting.

A grief support group gets dark with the newest release from horror writer Eric LaRocca. After the death of his husband, Simeon becomes enmeshed with The Wretches, whose intense methods to process the death of loved ones leads Simeon to a mysterious man who promises they can all get one last moment with a loved one for a steep price.

The graduate of a deadly academy is the protagonist of Mark Lawrence's newest novel. Rue, now an old woman, is finally at peace with her violent upbringing. But as soon as she thinks she's entered retirement, the sins of her past come back to haunt her.

Trees can drag you to your death. Artificial monsters stalk the lands. And alien men wander around town. John Maraintha is dropped on the planet Scythia and has to find a way to adapt and survive.

Fans of classic folktale retellings will enjoy this take on The Little Mermaid. Rather than following Ariel, it centers on her granddaughter, who is awash in complex politics after the assassination of her father. To save her family's legacy, she makes a deal with the famed sea-witch Ursla.

If you're a fan of The Substance, you may enjoy this new book. A young struggling writer named Maggie meets an established producer who's looking to revive her career. The solution to both of their problems is an experimental procedure–that takes Maggie's youth and gives it to the older producer–along with a $3 million payout that helps with Maggie's money troubles. But both women quickly realize that the blood transfusion is anything but a simple transaction.

A beloved actor in an epic fantasy franchise where much of the characters believe the world is real makes a bold choice to break out of the false reality the studio has built, and convince his co-stars to go with him.

The eighth, highly anticipated book in the Dungeon Crawler Carl series picks up on the tenth floor, where Carl and Donut try to make sense of the system AI's mysterious plans and learn more about why it calls the eleventh floor 'A Parade of Horribles'.

If you're yearning for an epic tale of political intrigue, this new Ann Leckie read is for you. #4812. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4811. The Simple Magic of Self-Affirmation

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 11, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

What if I told you that a five-minute activity can not only help people make positive changes, but also maintain those changes more than two years later?

A group of researchers conducted two studies with female university students who were dissatisfied with their weight.1,2 The participants completed questionnaires about their eating, exercise, ideal weight, confidence in their ability to lose weight, and concerns about their body; their height and weight were measured, and their body mass index (BMI) was calculated. They were also randomly assigned to complete one of two brief, self-directed activities, both unrelated to body weight, appearance, or weight loss: a "self-affirmation" activity or a neutral ("control") activity. They were given no guidance or counseling on diet, exercise, or weight loss methods.

About two months later, the participants returned to repeat the assessments. In both studies, women who had self-affirmed—and particularly, those whose BMI was high initially—weighed less than they did at their first visit, while the control group (who had not self-affirmed) weighed more. In the second study, women with high BMIs who had self-affirmed also reported more exercise, and they were observed eating more healthful foods than those who had not self-affirmed.

After another two years, the researchers reached out to the women in both studies and assessed them again.3 They found that high-BMI women who had self-affirmed at their first visit had kept their weight the same, whereas those who had not self-affirmed were continuing to gain more weight.

It may be hard to appreciate just how remarkable these results are. One of the most reliable findings in research on psychosocial interventions (counseling, therapy, advice, instruction, etc.) is that even when they’re effective in the short term, the results usually fade over time. What kind of brief activity, which had nothing directly to do with weight loss, could continue to have a positive effect more than two years later?

In motivational interviewing, affirming refers to the expression of appreciation or admiration for a person’s actions, intentions, strengths, or enduring characteristics.4 But in these studies, participants were not invited to affirm themselves in this way.

Rather, they were given a list of values—none of which were related to weight, health, or appearance—and asked to rank them in order of personal importance, and then write about a time when their most important value had been important to them and why it was important to them.5 That’s it: the intervention had nothing to do with weight loss, their efforts to lose weight, or how they felt about the whole subject; it simply asked them to think about what mattered most to them and describe how they had lived out that value at another time in their life.

These studies are part of a robust research literature that consistently demonstrates the positive effects of a variety of self-affirmation activities of this kind.6 In the area of health behavior change, for example, low-income, heavy cigarette smokers in the UK were more receptive to a novel anti-smoking message and expressed greater intention to change when they self-affirmed prior to receiving the message7; university students in China were more receptive to information on COVID-19 vaccines, and had higher vaccination intention, if they self-affirmed prior to receiving the information.8

The self-affirmation effect has also been found in the area of academic performance. Black middle school students who were randomly assigned to self-affirm had higher grade point averages (GPA) over 2 years than those who did not self-affirm; the largest effect was among low-achieving Black students, whereas GPA was unaffected in White students who self-affirmed.9 College women enrolled in Introductory Physics who were randomly assigned to self-affirm earned higher grades than did those who did not self-affirm; the largest effect was in women who wondered if the old stereotype that women are inferior to men in the study of science might be true.10

These last two studies hint at the source of self-affirmation’s power. The psychologist Claude Steele proposed that stereotype threat—the fear, felt by members of groups stigmatized as inferior in a particular area, that they may confirm the negative stereotype by performing poorly—can create a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy, interfering with their performance and resulting in the very outcome they dread.11 If this is so, an activity that reduces the threat could result in people performing up to their actual potential.

However, positive effects from self-affirmation activities have been found not only in members of stigmatized groups, but in a wide variety of populations and behaviors. So if self-affirmation works in all these cases by reducing a perceived threat, what sort of threat is it reducing? And why would writing about an important value and its role in your life reduce it?

I’ll take up these two important questions in part 2 of this series.

1. Logel, C. & Cohen, G.L. (2012). The role of the self in physical health: Testing the effect of a values-affirmation intervention on weight loss. Psychological Science, 23, 53-55.

2. Logel, C., Hall, W., Page-Gould, E., & Cohen, G.L. (2019). Why is it so hard to change? The role of self-integrity threat and affirmation in weight loss. European Journal of Social Psychology, 49, 748–759.

3. Logel, C., Kathmandub, A., & Cohen, G.L. (2019). Affirmation prevents long-term weight gain. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 81, 70–75.

4. Miller, W.R. & Rollnick, S. (2023). Motivational Interviewing: Helping People Change and Grow. 4th Edition. Guilford Press.

5. Harber, K. (1995). Sources of Validation Scale. Unpublished scale.

6. McQueen, A. & Klein, W.M.P. (2006). Experimental manipulations of self-affirmation: A systematic review. Self and Identity, 5, 289 – 354.

7. Armitage, C. J., Harris, P. R., Hepton, G., & Napper, L. (2008). Self-affirmation increases acceptance of health risk information among UK adult smokers with low socioeconomic status. Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, 22, 88-95.

8. Li, S., Xia, Y., Zhao, W., Miao, X., & Xu, Q. (2023). Self‑affirmation increases acceptance of information on COVID‑19 vaccines and promotes vaccination intention. Journal of Behavioral Medicine, 46, 303–310.

9. Cohen, G.L., Garcia, J., Purdie-Vaughns, V., Apfel, N., & Brzustoski, P. (2009). Recursive processes in self-affirmation: Intervening to close the minority achievement gap. Science, 324, 400-403.

10. Miyake, A., Kost-Smith, L.E., Finkelstein, N.D., Pollock, S.J., Cohen, G.L., & Ito, T.A. (2010). Reducing the gender achievement gap in college science: a classroom study of values affirmation. Science, 330, 1234–1237.

11. Steele, C.M. & Aronson, J. (1995). Stereotype threat and the intellectual test performance of African Americans. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69, 797–811.

#4810. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

#4809. The Next Generation of Weight-Loss Drugs Is Reshaping People’s Looks—And Not in a Flattering Way

WHEN YOU LOSE weight through traditional diet and exercise, you tend to see a gradual slimming down of your face. But when you add in gray-market peptides like retatrutide, you’re expediting the weight loss process. That also includes rapid fat loss in the face, leaving a sunken and hollowed-out look people are dubbing “reta face.”

Online Reddit communities on peptides and biohacking are packed with people commenting on changes to their facial appearance after taking retatrutide—a triple hormone agonist of the GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors that’s expected to become the next generation of weight-loss injections. One clinical trial found those taking retatrutide had more than double the weight loss of people taking Ozempic.

To be fair, “Ozempic face” has also been an issue. But with Eli Lilly expected to apply for FDA approval of retatrutide in early 2027 for obesity and other conditions, doctors say reta will likely cause more facial volume issues. Is there any way to prevent these unflattering side effects? We went straight to the doctors currently treating people with facial symptoms from GLPs.

WHILE RETA FACE isn’t an official medical diagnosis, it’s a real phenomenon. “The facial changes can be kind of dramatic,” says Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. But the lack of criteria has also caused some debate over what qualifies as reta face.

On the r/BodyHackGuide community (with over 87,000 contributors dubbed “Lab Rats”), reta face before-and-after posts are recurring discussion threads. Some describe reta face as a chiseled look after weight loss while Ozempic face is the more sickly face. Others argue that “reta face” and “Ozempic face” are simply two terms to describe the sunken look from your face losing fat.

“Reta face is the new Ozempic face,” says dermatologist Gary Goldenberg, MD. “Since retatrutide is a triple biologic agonist that produces more significant weight loss than GLP peptides, patients may have an even more exaggerated appearance of a sunken, aged look.”

That means cheeks can become flat and hollow, temples narrow, and undereye areas can look sunken and dark. “Facial bones can also become more prominent as fat disappears,” says Dr. Goldenberg. “The skin can thin, as collagen and elastic fibers have less underlying fat plumping them up.”

Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research in dermatology at Mount Sinai Hospital, says the shape of your face changes with any significant weight loss—it’s just more apparent when someone is on a weight-loss medication.

ABSOLUTELY. DR. ZEICHNER says minimizing the appearance of facial wasting is all about losing weight slowly—even when taking a GLP-1 or reta. While you can’t target specific areas for fat loss, Dr. Goldenberg recommends pacing yourself while still getting plenty of protein on your plate and being selective about meals that have enough nutrients.

If you already have reta face and the appearance bothers you, Dr. Goldenberg recommends seeing a dermatologist. “Collagen stimulators and fillers are a very common treatment for this problem,” he says. “Volume can be restored and contouring can be improved with these treatments.”

#4807. Five Reasons Marsha Linehan Will Always Be a Legend

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 12, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

The field of clinical psychology lost a giant this week with the passing of Marsha Linehan, the psychologist who developed dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and fundamentally changed how we understand and treat borderline personality disorder (BPD).

For decades, people with BPD were considered among the most difficult patients to treat. In fact, many clinicians believed that these patients were untreatable. Linehan proved them wrong by developing a better treatment. Since its publication in 1993, DBT has saved countless lives and inspired generations of clinicians and researchers.

As a clinical psychologist whose own career has been shaped by her work, I've been reflecting on what made Linehan such an extraordinary figure. Here are five reasons her legacy will endure.

When Marsha began her work, people experiencing chronic suicidality and severe emotional dysregulation were often viewed as too difficult or too risky to treat. Rather than accepting that these patients couldn't be helped, she set out to develop a treatment that could get the job done.

The result was dialectical behavior therapy, a structured treatment that combined cognitive-behavioral strategies with acceptance-based approaches drawn from Zen practice. DBT taught people practical skills to manage overwhelming emotions, navigate relationships, and build lives worth living.

Marsha was also a scientist who understood the importance of testing whether her approach actually worked. Through rigorous clinical trials, she demonstrated that even people experiencing severe and persistent suicidal behaviors could benefit from treatment.

In doing so, she challenged the longstanding assumption that BPD was untreatable and helped establish a new standard of care.

Patients with BPD were frequently described as manipulative, attention-seeking, or resistant to treatment.

Marsha challenged these labels by encouraging clinicians to understand the function of behavior. Actions that seemed manipulative or irrational often served a purpose, such as escaping overwhelming emotions or getting important needs met.

Rather than blaming patients for these behaviors, therapists could work to understand what was reinforcing them and teach more effective ways to achieve the same goals.

In 2011, Marsha publicly shared her own history of severe suffering, suicidality, and psychiatric hospitalization in a New York Times profile.

This revelation had a huge impact. Here was one of the world's most influential clinical psychologists disclosing that she had once experienced profound psychological distress herself.

Marsha later shared more of her story in her memoir, Building a Life Worth Living. She recalled a patient asking her, “Are you one of us?” For people experiencing profound psychological suffering, knowing that someone who had faced similar struggles could go on to build such an extraordinary life offered a powerful source of hope.

She was living proof that recovery was possible.

One of Marsha's most important contributions was her emphasis on dialectical thinking, the ability to recognize that two seemingly contradictory things can both be true.

You can accept yourself as you are and work to change.

You can validate someone's suffering and hold them accountable for their behavior.

You can do your best and need to do better.

This was a major shift in how therapists approached treatment. Rather than choosing between validating someone's experience and encouraging them to change, Marsha showed us how to do both. This allowed therapists to approach even the most challenging behaviors with compassion while still helping clients take responsibility for building better lives.

Marsha's influence extends well beyond the people who received DBT. She trained and inspired generations of clinicians and researchers who have continued building on her work.

DBT was the first treatment I learned as a graduate student. Today, I supervise DBT in that same clinic, and Marsha's work continues to shape my own work, BPD Compass.

I first met Marsha when she stopped by my poster at a conference. I was a graduate student presenting BPD research, and I completely fan-girled. It was really cool that she took time to look through the BPD-themed posters and offer encouragement.

Years later, I interviewed with Marsha for a postdoctoral position. Although my career ultimately took me in a different direction, she still agreed to co-mentor my first National Institute of Mental Health grant.

Marsha generously gave her time and encouragement—multiply the experience by the generations of clinicians and researchers she mentored, and you begin to appreciate the reach of her influence.

Marsha Linehan fundamentally changed what clinicians believed was possible for people with BPD by giving them tools that actually worked for these clients.

Despite these advances, too many people with BPD still struggle to access effective treatment. Making effective BPD treatment available to more people is one way we can honor her legacy.

Marsha's influence will live on through the people whose lives she saved and the generations of clinicians and researchers she inspired.

Marsha's influence on my work continues through BPD Compass, a treatment my colleagues and I developed to help make evidence-based care for BPD more accessible.

#4806. Bigger, badder Section 179 tax deduction could POWER UP fleet electrification [update]

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers, it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks, electric vocational trucks, battery electric reefer trailers, and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, magic pixie dust, anything else.

There’s been some additional movement on the tax front since our original article, too. Earlier this year, the IRS issued Notice 2026-11, providing additional guidance on the permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025. That means that eligible businesses might be able to combine Section 179 expensing with bonus depreciation when ordering qualifying fleet equipment – and ordering is the key word. The IRS has specific rules for determining when equipment is considered acquired under a written, binding contract, and your tax professional and truck dealer can probably help you figure out a way to make those rules work in your favor.

You can check out the original article (with a few corrections sprinkled in to align with the latest guidance from Notice 2026-11 and Publication 946) below. Give it a read, read the disclaimer twice, then let us know what you think in the comments.

After the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (Section 45W) expired on September 30, the “experts” rushed out predictions of an EV sales slowdown in Q4. But, with over 6,800 pages in the Internal Revenue Code still in play, a turbocharged Section 179 tax deduction could still power a strong year for commercial EVs.

The One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 gutted America’s energy independence goals and ensuring its auto industry would fall even further behind the Chinese in the EV race, but the loss of Section 45W wasn’t the only change written into the IRS’ rulebook. Section 179, an immediate expense reduction that business owners can take on depreciable equipment assets, has been made significantly more powerful for 2025.

The section 179 expense deduction is limited to such items as cars, office equipment, business machinery, and computers. This speedy deduction can provide substantial tax relief for business owners who are purchasing startup equipment.

The revised Section 179 tax credit (or, more accurately, expense reduction) allows for a 100% deduction for equipment purchases has doubled to $2.5 million, with a phase-out kicking in at $4 million of capital investments that drops to zero at $6.5 million. That can be applied to new and used vehicles, as well as charging infrastructure, battery energy storage systems, specialized tools, and more (as long as they’re new to you).

“But wait,” as they say. “There’s more!” A revised Section 168(k) also allows for bonus depreciation on eligible equipment and property, accelerating depreciation for a reduced tax burden.

Section 179 and bonus depreciation aren’t mutually exclusive, either, which means that businesses don’t have to exceed the Section 179 spending cap to be able to take advantage of both. A fleet operator can elect to expense a portion of a qualifying vehicle or equipment purchase under Section 179, then apply bonus depreciation to the remaining eligible basis.

With 100% bonus depreciation restored for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, that combination could allow businesses to deduct the entire qualifying business-use cost of an electric truck or other commercial equipment in the first year, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and limitations.

It’s a bit convoluted (what good tax code isn’t?), but these tax incentives are great for businesses looking to buy enough electric equipment assets to exceed the Section 179 spending limit – and, given the new Uber/Tesla semi truck purchase plan, the continued growth of the electric terminal tractor market, and the willingness of several utilities to incentivize both electric commercial vehicles and the deployment of smart EV charging infrastructure, that number may be bigger than you think.

Tax law is weird. Not only are there Federal tax laws and rules that need to be followed, but state and even local county and city rules, as well. As such, you want to make sure they don’t get you the way the got Capone.

Even worse, your favorite journalist (Hi!) is probably an idiot. Get a certified accountant and tax law expert to help walk you through the dirtier details of your specific scenario – but don’t let the complexity of human interaction slow you down, either. The really rich guys you know pay pennies on the tax dollar compared to you and me, because they’re not afraid to ask their accountants for help.

As a tax CPA, I cringe when I see "Sec 179" and the word "credit" put together. It is grossly inaccurate to say that Sec 179 is a tax credit.

Sec 179 and bonus depreciation are nothing new. OBBBA just raised the 179 maximum up, but the deductibility, specifically for heavy vehicles like semis, is unchanged.

The TL;DR version, though, is this: there’s still plenty of incentives out there for fleet operators looking to electrify their operations.

#4805. The 7 Best Electric Toothbrushes for Men in 2026, Tested by Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Cleaner, healthier teeth with picks for every budget and style of brushing.

YOU ALREADY KNOW you need to brush at least twice a day, no matter what toothpaste or mouthwash you use. But technique matters just as much. Even for me—a grooming editor who writes about this stuff—it can feel like a chore. In the morning, I brush before coffee when I’m barely awake. At night, I’m wiped out from the day or drifting off for less wholesome reasons. That’s why I love electric toothbrushes: they simplify brushing and deliver a better clean by doing most of the work for you.

Unlike manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrushes use vibrations and automated head movement to remove plaque and debris. Many models include smart programs for whitening or gum care, interchangeable heads for sensitive or deep cleaning, and built-in timers. Some of the latest options even feature AI that tracks your brushing and suggests improvements.

But the main selling point of electric toothbrushes is their ability to clean more thoroughly and efficiently than manual options, using power and vibrations no hand can match. Top-tier electric toothbrushes can be pricey, but they’re an investment in your smile. It’s the closest you can get to a dentist-level clean at home.

For the past two years, the Oral-B Series 10 has been listed at the top of this list. It remains the best overall electric toothbrush; however, it’s currently sold out everywhere due to this demand. The model that immediately preceded it, the iO Series 9, is the next best thing. It features many of the same features and power, just with a less high-tech charging mount (which may be a benefit for some who prefer something lighter and less complicated).

Series 9 is similarly a premium electric toothbrush packed with advanced features designed to elevate your oral care routine. Just like the 10, there are seven customizable modes—including Daily Clean, Sensitive, Super Sensitive, Intense, Gum Care, Tongue Clean, and Whitening—this brush adapts to your needs, whether you have sensitive gums or want a deep clean. Its oscillating, vibrating round brush head provides a powerful yet gentle clean, and the built-in pressure sensor ensures you're brushing with the right amount of force, lighting up red (too strong), blue (too weak), or green (just right) based on your pressure.

The Series 9 pairs with a companion app to track your brushing in real time across 16 zones of the mouth, offering instant feedback and a visual map of missed areas. I’m not a huge tech junkie, especially when it comes to something like brushing my teeth, since I just want to get it over with quickly. But this is one of the few apps that genuinely adds value, with accurate tracking, clear visuals, and brushing reminders.

Even if you skip the app, the built-in display shows your selected mode and a timer, though the latter is easier to read in the app. That being said, it’s nearly impossible to achieve a 100 percent clean according to the app (I usually aim for between 80 and 90) without brushing for five or more minutes, which is not recommended because it can damage enamel. If you’re a perfectionist, this will prove annoying.

In terms of design, the Series 9 is sleek and solid, and comes with a sturdy travel case. It charges in just three hours (significantly faster than most others on this list) and comes with four replacement heads, which should cover your first year of use if you replace them every three months, as dentists advise.

If you prefer sonic, this toothbrush offers nearly the same level of features and effectiveness as the Oral-B iO Series 9. At $340, it's also one of the most expensive electric toothbrushes, but the price includes five modes and three intensity settings to fully customize your brushing experience, along with an innovative charging cup.

Interchangeable brush heads, specifically designed for tasks like whitening or tongue cleaning, also help you achieve optimal results with minimal effort. Similar to the Series 9, it also has app-enabled smart modes that provide personalized feedback on your brushing habits and overall progress. Plus, the charging travel case makes it easy to travel while protecting your investment.

Women’s Health Associate Style and Commerce Editor Shannen Zitz has been using this toothbrush for the past year and says it’s the cleanest her teeth have ever felt. “I’ve long been using an electric toothbrush, so I didn’t expect to be too blown away by this one. I was wrong.” She likes how it pairs multiple brush heads, cleaning modes, and a timer with real-time app feedback to keep her brushing technique on track. The sleek charging cup also makes storage and charging effortless, even on a tiny sink, she says.

Read More: Are Electric Toothbrushes Better?

Men’s Health Associate Producer Janie Booth says the round, oscillating head reminds her of the tool dental hygienists use to polish teeth during a professional cleaning. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both of which are easy to pack. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long.

Booth says she’s used it for a month without recharging once. If your biggest concern is avoiding charging as much as possible, the Rev is your best bet. The battery even outperforms the Oral-B iO Series 9 and Philips Sonicare DiamondClean, both of which are roughly $300 more expensive.

I’ve used all three as my daily driver at different times, and the Rev battery lasts at least a week longer. You can expect to get at least 5 weeks from a single full charge with twice-a-day use. The rest of its offerings are pretty minimal, though, again, this will be welcomed by newcomers. It only offers three levels of intensity, but none are too strong for sensitive teeth.

However, they’re not quite as powerful as the most intense settings on Oral-B and Philips, though they are close. The Oral-B iO Series 9 offers about 10,500 oscillations per minute on its Daily Clean setting, while the Rev goes up to 9,630 oscillations per minute. Considering the $300 price difference between the two, the slight dip is a worthy trade-off.

Before I upgraded to an electric, I was a devotee of Colgate’s Active Prevention Foaming Toothbrush. The heads are as soft as they come, and the handle fits perfectly in my hand. Naturally, I was thrilled when the brand made an electric version, adding vibration to those two core features. To be clear, this is battery-powered, so it’s not rechargeable. But you also don’t need to worry about recharging it every couple of weeks. I get a little more than a month out of each set of batteries (two AAAs), so while it’s under $15 at first, I plan to spend more over time.

Still, I haven’t tried a battery-powered toothbrush that lasts that long without sputtering or losing efficiency, like Colgate’s can. It’s not the most powerful electric toothbrush, as Colgate doesn’t even list its vibrations per minute (which usually means it’s nothing to write home about). But I’ve yet to find a battery-powered toothbrush that can compete with the power of rechargeable options, so it’s inherent to the design.

No matter your background, everyone shares one truth: we all lie to our dentists about flossing. They see through it, and they roll their eyes for good reason. Daily flossing is essential, which is why Waterpik built a toothbrush with an integrated water flosser. Its all-in-one design lets you brush and floss at the same time, saving effort while leaving your teeth feeling dentist-clean.

The brush includes two intensity modes and a timer, but the standout is the built-in Waterpik. You can brush with or without the water flosser, though why skip it? While it doesn’t offer the smart features of higher-end models, the unique water flosser justifies its higher price tag. Plus, its 30,000 vibrations per minute match those of the similarly priced Zina45. In that sense, it’s like the water flosser is free.

This toothbrush offers 33,000 vibrations per minute, four custom settings, a two-minute timer, and soft, nylon bristles. It’s everything you need for a decent electric toothbrush. However, there are two features that help it stand out. For one, the magnetic USB touch charger is super convenient, making recharging as simple as any option on this list. As someone who regularly forgets to recharge his devices, I appreciate how easy this one makes the process.

It also comes with a polishing head, one of the few electric toothbrushes that do. This tiny rubber head is designed to make your teeth look smoother and shinier by focusing on surface stains and plaque removal rather than deep cleaning between teeth. I use mine after brushing, even if I brush with a separate toothbrush, to complete the full at-home dentist-level clean. It also comes with four replaceable polishing heads, so you won’t have to worry about replacing them for some time.

At first, the smaller toothbrush head on the Suri 2.0 felt less effective than the OG model, but over time, it delivers the same clean. The brush comes with a compact stand and a travel case, both designed for travel. It doesn’t include a wall plug—just a USB cord—but the battery lasts impressively long. It’s the only other electric toothbrush we’ve tested that lasts over a month on a single charge, though I find it’s a couple of days shorter than the Quip Rev.

This brush delivers 33,000 vibrations per minute yet remains whisper-quiet. Its sleek case hides a UV-C light that kills 99 percent of germs on the brush head, keeping it clean wherever you take it. Plus, the head and bristles are eco-friendly, made from recyclable, plant-based cornstarch and castor oil. Overall, it’s powerful, sustainable, and travel-ready.

When choosing an electric toothbrush, you’ll need to decide between a sonic or oscillating brush head. There isn’t one right answer; it just comes down to preference.

Toothbrushes have gone smart, too. Most models include the basics—a strong motor and a built-in timer—but many now add extras like brushing modes, pressure sensors, and even AI to track your habits and coach you to improve. The right features depend on what matters most to you.

Brushing your teeth is personal, shaped by your own needs and quirks. To find the best electric toothbrushes for every sensitivity and style, we tapped a wide group of Men’s Health testers. I spoke with dentists about their go-to brands, pulled in feedback from our original 2019 guide, and compiled a list of top contenders. I then distributed these toothbrushes to writers and editors, each of whom tested them for at least a month to judge comfort, ease of use, and long-term effectiveness. Based on that feedback, here are the eight best electric toothbrushes for men in 2026.

As with manual toothbrushes, electric toothbrush heads need to be replaced every few months. Because the latter tend to be more expensive, this makes owning electric models more expensive. I recommend buying the heads in bulk when available, as this can make for pretty substantial savings. Electric toothbrushes have more nooks and crevices than their manual counterparts, which means they require a little extra daily maintenance.

This means carefully rinsing them after every use to stave off funky toothpaste and spit residue. It’s also worth actually removing the brush head from time to time to wipe the attachment point where the head meets the handle. A cotton swab or even your old toothbrush is usually enough to do the trick.

It’s tempting to just toss old toothbrushes and toothbrush heads in the trash once they’ve outlived their usefulness. But they’re actually perfect for detailed cleaning work that requires moderately stiff bristles to clean out tight spaces. Think: Shower heads, hiking boots, bathroom grout, your dishwasher filter, bird feeders—you get the idea.
